candidates.title: Self-reported confidence in biorisk management after a multisectoral step-down training in Botswana: a cross-sectional post-training evaluation of 26 professionals from 24 institutions
candidates.abstract: Background Biosafety and biosecurity capacity across Africa remains low relative to expanding laboratory infrastructure. Continental averages on the Africa Health Security Index stand at 14.9 of 100 for biosecurity and 18.2 for biosafety. The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) Regional Training and Certification Program seeks to address this by certifying regional subject matter experts who deliver training within their own countries. Whether such step-down training reaches beyond the clinical laboratory sector, and where its effects are weakest, has not been well described. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional post-training evaluation of a seven-module biorisk management course delivered in Botswana in 2024 to 26 professionals drawn from 24 institutions across seven sectors, recruited under a One Health framework spanning human/animal health, food safety, environment, defense, regulation, transport, and academia. Curriculum content was adapted from the Sandia National Laboratories core biorisk management materials. Participants completed a 61-item, 5-point Likert scale questionnaire post-course. The outcome measured was self-reported confidence, expressed as the proportion selecting agree or strongly agree (positive response rate) and the mean Likert score. Results Positive response rates were highest for conceptual and procedural items and lowest for items requiring independent institutional action. Definitional and personal protective equipment items reached 100%, including exposure route identification and donning/doffing procedures. However, confidence fell to 76.9% for planning institutional biorisk implementation steps, to 76.0% for developing risk-based facility maintenance strategies, and to 73.1% for executing the seven-step infectious substance shipping process and managing biological transport. By sector, positive response rates ranged from 81.1% to 100%, but the rankings changed when the mean Likert score was used instead. Conclusion This single multisectoral course yielded high confidence in conceptual and personal-protection items, but lower confidence in institutional implementation, regulated transport, and facility maintenance. The self-reported design limits inferences about knowledge gain. Practicum-based instruction and post-training mentorship are candidate approaches for future evaluation.

candidates.title: Quality, reliability, and readability of large language model responses to questions about immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated myocarditis: A cross-sectional study
candidates.abstract: Abstract Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated myocarditis (ICI-M) is a rare but often fatal immune-related adverse event. Large language models (LLMs) have provided new opportunities for patient education, yet whether they can effectively support patient education in ICI-M remains unknown. In this study, we submitted 20 standardized ICI-M-related patient questions to five LLMs (ChatGPT-5.5, Gemini-3.5 Flash, DeepSeek-V4, Qwen 3.7, and Doubao), generating 100 responses. Model performance was evaluated using the Global Quality Score (GQS), modified DISCERN (mDISCERN), Quality Analysis of Medical Artificial Intelligence (QAMAI), Ensuring Quality Information for Patients (EQIP), Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool understandability and actionability scores (PEMAT-U and PEMAT-A), and six readability indices. Significant inter-model differences were observed across most quality and readability metrics, and no single model outperformed the others across all dimensions. DeepSeek-V4 achieved the highest mDISCERN score [5.00 (IQR, 4.00–5.00)], whereas ChatGPT-5.5 achieved the highest PEMAT-A score [40.00 (IQR, 35.00–45.00)]. Readability was suboptimal, with a mean FKGL of 16.60 ± 2.64. Correlation analyses demonstrated information quality, usability, and readability represented correlated but distinct evaluation dimensions. While LLMs may serve as adjunctive tools for ICI-M patient education, substantial optimization of content accessibility and actionability is required prior to clinical implementation.

candidates.title: Large language model-generated vs. human-authored assessment items in education: systematic review and meta-analysis with a focus on health professional education
candidates.abstract: Purpose Assessment is crucial in health professional education (HPE) but is resource-intensive to create. Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential solution by generating assessment items; however, a comprehensive synthesis of their psychometric quality is lacking in HPE. Design/methodology/approach We systematically searched the electronic databases and included studies generating assessment items using any LLM and reporting psychometric outcomes. The primary outcomes were item difficulty index, discrimination index, distractor effectiveness and risk of nonfunctioning distractors (NFDs). Pooled estimates (Hedges' g or odds ratios [OR] with 95% confidence intervals [CIs]) were calculated using a random-effects model. Surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) for ranking the test item generating methods was estimated. Grades of Recommendation, Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach was used for determining the strength of evidence. Findings Fifty-four studies were included. In direct comparisons with human-generated items (92.8% of studies in HPE), LLM-generated items had a significantly higher difficulty index (pooled g: 0.40, 95% CI: 0.23 to 0.57), indicating they were easier and had significantly higher odds of containing NFDs (OR: 1.86, 95% CI: 1.27 to 2.73). The discrimination index was not significantly different (g: –0.21, 95% CI: –0.49 to 0.07), but distractor effectiveness was poorer (g: –0.65, 95% CI: –1.31 to 0). When evaluated alone, 67% of LLM-items were accurate or required only minor revisions, but 37% of distractors were NFDs. SUCRA analyses consistently ranked human-generated items as superior across all critical psychometric parameters. Evidence certainty ranged between very low and moderate. Originality/value LLMs can generate assessment items efficiently, but their current output is psychometrically inferior to human-authored items, being significantly easier and containing more flawed distractors. While a substantial proportion of items are useable with minor edits, sophisticated prompt engineering and expert-led review are essential to ensure the creation of valid and reliable assessments for HPE.

candidates.title: Evaluating the effectiveness of staff training in trauma-informed care in a community older adult mental health service: a service evaluation
candidates.abstract: Purpose This study aims to assess the impact of a trauma-informed care (TIC) training programme within an NHS older adult (OA) community mental health service, addressing a gap in trauma-informed implementation for later life populations. Design/methodology/approach A mixed-methods, within-subjects design was used. Staff self-rated their TIC knowledge and confidence pre- and post-training using Likert scales (N = 32), and post-training questionnaire responses were analysed using both deductive and inductive content analysis. Findings Wilcoxon signed-rank tests indicated statistically significant increases in staff knowledge and confidence post-training, both with large effect sizes. Qualitative findings showed strong uptake of core TIC principles – particularly “Safety”, “Trustworthiness”, “Collaboration” and “Empowerment”. Barriers to trauma-informed practice included fear of re-traumatisation and time constraints. Feedback identified the training as relevant and interactive, though improvements were suggested around dementia applicability and content density. Practical implications The findings of this study highlight the value of contextualised, experiential TIC training and the need for structural changes to support sustainable implementation. Tailoring content to dementia care may improve relevance in OA services. Originality/value The evaluation contributes novel evidence on embedding TIC in community OA mental health settings, supporting scalable implementation.

candidates.title: Vision-driven retrieval-augmented decision support for plant disease diagnosis using EfficientNetV2 and large language models
candidates.abstract: Abstract Accurate and timely plant disease diagnosis is essential for sustainable agricultural production and precision farming. However, most existing agricultural decision support systems treat visual disease diagnosis and agronomic recommendation generation as separate processes, either providing image classification results alone or generating recommendations with large language models that are not grounded in domain-specific knowledge. To address this limitation, this study introduces EffiToRag, an end-to-end decision support framework that integrates an EfficientNetV2-based visual diagnosis module with a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture. Rather than relying solely on free-text queries for disease-level retrieval, the proposed approach uses the disease class predicted by EfficientNetV2 as the primary key for retrieving the corresponding record from a structured agronomic knowledge base constructed from peer-reviewed scientific publications and official phytopathological guidelines. The visual diagnosis module was trained using Progressive Training and Class-Aware Tiered Augmentation (CATA) to account for differences in class representation. On a held-out test set comprising 11,621 images across 60 plant health classes, EfficientNetV2-M achieved 99.13% accuracy and a Macro F1 score of 0.9889, with an inference time of 4.39 ms per image on the evaluated GPU. For 500 user queries, the system selected query-relevant knowledge fields with a precision of 0.972 and a recall of 0.985. The factual-consistency assessment combined GPT-4-based evaluation and manual expert review of a random sample of 100 diagnostic reports and yielded a mean factual-consistency score of 0.99. The experts also assigned these reports a mean applicability score of 4.85/5.0. These findings show that visual disease classification, structured agronomic knowledge retrieval, and LLM-based recommendation generation can be integrated within a single decision support pipeline for precision agriculture.

candidates.title: Understanding the Fundamental Design Decisions of Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a critical technique for enhancing large language model (LLM) capabilities. However, practitioners face significant challenges when making RAG deployment decisions. While existing research prioritizes algorithmic innovations, a systematic gap persists in understanding fundamental engineering tradeoffs that determine RAG success. We present the first comprehensive study of three universal RAG deployment decisions: whether to deploy RAG, how much information to retrieve, and how to integrate retrieved knowledge effectively. Through systematic experiments across three LLMs and six datasets spanning question answering and code generation tasks, we reveal critical insights: (1) RAG deployment must be highly selective, with variable recall thresholds and failure modes affecting up to 12.6% of samples even with perfect documents. (2) Optimal retrieval volume exhibits task-dependent behavior—QA tasks show universal patterns (5–10 documents optimal) while code generation requires scenario-specific optimization. (3) Knowledge integration effectiveness depends on task and model characteristics, with code generation benefiting significantly from prompting methods while question answering shows minimal improvement. These findings demonstrate that universal RAG strategies prove inadequate. Effective RAG systems require context-aware design decisions based on task characteristics and model capabilities. Our analysis provides evidence-based guidance for practitioners and establishes foundational insights for principled RAG deployment. Our code, data, and artifacts are publicly available at https://github.com/ShengmingZ/RAG_Benchmark_Code_QA .

candidates.title: GeoKG-Ore: Knowledge Graph-Augmented Large Language Models for Intelligent Gold Exploration
candidates.abstract: Abstract Gold exploration is an evidence-intensive spatial decision problem in which geological structures, host lithologies, alteration assemblages, geochemical anomalies, geophysical responses, and remote-sensing observations must be interpreted jointly across heterogeneous spatial scales. Conventional mineral prospectivity mapping (MPM) models can learn nonlinear associations from these data, yet their predictions are often weakly connected to explicit metallogenic mechanisms, source provenance, and the sequential decisions made during exploration. Large language models (LLMs) provide flexible geological knowledge interaction, but their parametric knowledge and unconstrained text generation are insufficient for spatially grounded, uncertainty-aware target delineation. We introduce GeoKG-Ore, a knowledge graph-augmented LLM framework that formulates intelligent gold exploration as closed-loop inference over a provenance-aware spatial knowledge graph. Its central mechanism is a query-conditioned probabilistic geological field that jointly governs prospectivity estimation, graph-consistency constraints, and value-of-information evidence acquisition. A budget-aware policy selects the next evidence source according to expected posterior utility, while a provenance-constrained generator converts verified graph paths and spatial evidence into auditable exploration reports. We evaluate GeoKG-Ore using public mineral-occurrence, geological, geochemical, geophysical, and satellite data sources. On a benchmark comprising 36,480 analysis cells and 428 verified occurrence anchors, GeoKG-Ore achieves an AUROC of 0.913, an AUPRC of 0.612, and a recall of 0.574 within the top 5\% of the explored area, with an expected calibration error of 0.038. The results support the value of coupling spatial geological knowledge, uncertainty-aware prospectivity inference, and budget-aware evidence acquisition for evidence-grounded gold exploration.

candidates.title: Construction of Reliable Vertical Large Language Model Systems for Sustainable Catalysis: From Evidence‐Bound Knowledge Extraction to Closed‐Loop Catalyst Discovery
candidates.abstract: Catalysis is central to energy conversion and green chemistry, but its development is constrained by fragmented literature data, complex reaction systems, difficult mechanistic identification, and reliance on empirical trial and error. Large language models (LLMs), with capabilities in unstructured text understanding, multisource knowledge integration, reasoning, and tool invocation, have been increasingly applied to literature extraction, characterization analysis, mechanistic hypothesis generation, catalyst recommendation, condition optimization, and automated experimentation. However, catalytic tasks are highly specialized, condition‐dependent, and validation‐intensive, making general‐purpose LLMs insufficient for traceable, verifiable, safe, and controllable research. This review summarizes recent progress in applying LLMs to key catalytic tasks and discusses their reliability requirements. We further propose a catalysis‐oriented vertical LLM framework consisting of “task definition–evidence access–constraint control–model adaptation–validation evaluation–feedback updating.” By integrating evidence‐constrained knowledge extraction, constraint‐aware decision‐making, and feedback‐driven closed‐loop optimization, this framework aims to reduce low‐value trial‐and‐error experiments, unnecessary reagent consumption, energy input, and waste generation, thereby supporting reliable and sustainable catalysis research.

candidates.title: Manifestation-Guided Adaptation of CT Foundation Model for Early Neurological Prognosis after ECPR
candidates.abstract: Purpose. To develop a data-efficient, clinically guided transfer-learning framework for hyperacute neurological outcome prediction from head CT in patients undergoing extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) after cardiac arrest by leveraging free-text radiology report. Methods. This retrospective study included 683 patients with available CT examination and radiology reports from December 2015 to November 2025. The primary outcome distinguished favorable neurological outcomes (Cerebral Performance Category [CPC] 1-2) from neurological death due to brain death or cerebral herniation (CPC 5). A cross-attention adaptor jointly learned to predict neurological outcome and five report-derived manifestations of brain injury from a frozen pretrained head CT encoder. Outcome prediction used CT images alone at inference. The manifestation-guided adaptor, trained with and without additional patients who contributed only manifestation labels, was compared with outcome-only adaptor and two pooled-feature baselines. Performance was summarized as mean ± SD across five held-out folds. Results. Of 683 patients, 197 were eligible for outcome evaluation (63 with favorable outcomes and 134 with neurological death), and 486 formed the manifestation-only cohort. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.918 ± 0.044 for the outcome-only adaptor. The manifestation-guided adaptor achieved an AUROC of 0.927 ± 0.042. With additional manifestation-only training data, the adaptor achieved the mean AUROC (0.929 ± 0.037), specificity (93.7% ± 6.5%), with a sensitivity of 79.9% ± 9.2%. Conclusion. Manifestation-guided adaptation outperforms outcome-only adaptation for neurological outcome prediction from hyperacute head CT after ECPR. Report-derived manifestation labels enabled training with additional examinations without eligible outcome labels while preserving CT-only prediction.

candidates.title: Benchmarking LLMs for Unit Test Generation from Real-World Functions
candidates.abstract: Recently, large language models (LLMs) have shown great promise in automating unit test generation, significantly reducing the manual effort required by developers. To effectively evaluate the capabilities of LLMs in this domain, it is crucial to have a well-designed benchmark that accurately reflects real-world scenarios and mitigates common pitfalls. Existing LLM test generation benchmarks are limited by two critical drawbacks: data contamination and structurally simple function code. As a result, scientific conclusions drawn from empirical studies using these benchmarks may be compromised. The evidence presented may be biased due to contamination and may fail to generalize beyond toy programs due to structural simplicity. To address these problems, we introduce ULT (UnLeakedTestbench), a new benchmark specifically designed for function-level unit test generation from real-world Python functions. ULT is constructed through a multi-stage curation process that ensures high cyclomatic complexity and mitigates test case contamination. With 3,909 carefully selected function-level tasks, ULT provides a more realistic and challenging evaluation of LLMs’ test generation capabilities. We also provide PLT (PreLeakedTestbench), a pair of ULT benchmarks with leaked tests designed to enable a controlled analysis of memorization versus reasoning in test generation. Based on the two datasets, we conduct a large-scale empirical study involving 12 state-of-the-art LLMs, comparing their performance against established benchmarks. Our evaluation results demonstrate that ULT is significantly more challenging. For example, test cases generated by LLMs only achieve 41.32%, 45.10%, 30.22%, and 40.21% for accuracy, statement coverage, branch coverage, and mutation score on average for all LLMs, respectively. These results are substantially lower than the corresponding metrics on TestEval (91.79%, 92.18%, 82.04%, and 49.69%) and PLT (47.07%, 55.13%, 40.07%, and 50.80%). In addition, different from existing benchmarks, ULT shows a strong correlation between test generation performance and code generation performance. For example, the correlation coefficient between the coding ability and test generation performance ( \(Pass@1\) ) on ULT is 0.79 (p = 0.002), while it is only 0.56 (p = 0.059) and 0.52 (p = 0.080) on TestEval and PLT, respectively. This indicates that ULT more effectively measures the generalization ability of LLMs. We also make ULT and evaluation results publicly available to foster further research (To preserve the integrity of the benchmark and prevent test case leakage into future LLM training sets, we do not release the ground-truth tests. Instead, we provide the complete evaluation results for all models benchmarked in this article. This allows researchers to compare new models against our findings without compromising the benchmark). ULT is available at https://github.com/huangd1999/UnLeakedTestBench .

candidates.title: Paradigm Evolution and Engineering Selection of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) suffer from two persistent problems in their parametric knowledge: update lag and factual deviation, which hinder their deployment in professional domains. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) connects external corpora at inference time, expanding the knowledge boundary without modifying model parameters, and has become the mainstream solution for enterprise knowledge bases, intelligent question answering, and document understanding. This paper divides RAG technology into four stages along its design focus: naive retrieval, precise retrieval, adaptive routing, and agentic reasoning, and examines the principal contradictions and new costs of each stage. On this basis, a hierarchical evolution framework is proposed that cross-compares six levels—retrieval, knowledge, fusion, generation, conflict arbitration, and engineering evaluation—against the four stages, identifying gaps in existing research, especially the unresolved arbitration of multi-source contradictory documents across all stages. The paper also discusses applicable boundaries: when knowledge is already well mastered by the model, when the context window suffices to cover the full corpus, or when the knowledge base is small and sparsely updated, adding a retrieval link only increases latency and noise. Finally, selection guidance is provided along three dimensions: accuracy, computational cost, and robustness, serving as a reference for engineering design and future research.

candidates.title: Large Language Models and Their Architectures for Machine Translation
candidates.abstract: Machine translation (MT) is the automatic conversion of text or speech from one language to another without human intervention. It has evolved from rule-based systems to data-driven methodologies, with neural machine translation (NMT) being a pivotal advancement in translation. Transformer is an encoder–decoder-based deep neural network, which is specifically designed for NMT. Large language models (LLMs) are based on transformer architecture and have deep bidirectional encoding and attention heads, enabling them to learn cross-lingual relationships. LLMs can perform translation through zero-shot and few-shot prompting. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is another way to use LLMs for MT systems, relying on knowledge sources like knowledge graphs and unstructured text documents that do not require specific training. Fine-tuning pretrained LLMs on a specific corpus can improve the efficacy of MT systems. LoRA (low-rank adaptation) and QLoRA algorithms can be used for fine-tuning parameters, reducing memory footprint requirements.

candidates.title: Scalable Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems for Educational Question Answering
candidates.abstract: AI tutors powered by Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) are increasingly used in education, but their reliability depends on retrieving appropriate instructional content. This study quantifies RAG performance in an educational setting using benchmarks of varying complexity derived from a biotechnology curriculum. We began with a baseline RAG system evaluated on a manually constructed question–answer benchmark, then introduced automated benchmark generation to scale evaluation across RAG configurations and identify the most impactful design choices. We further evaluated the best-performing configuration on textbook-section benchmarks labeled by Bloom's Taxonomy and Webb's Depth of Knowledge. Results show that architectural choices such as retrieval strategy and chunking were associated with larger performance differences than parameter-level adjustments, with Milvus hybrid retrieval achieving higher success rates than Pinecone dense retrieval in this benchmark. Full-textbook retrieval also improved performance on some higher-difficulty questions compared to section-limited search. Together, these findings underscore the importance of systematically evaluating retrieval reliability for AI tutors in complex biotechnology domains.

candidates.title: RoadVerse: A Domain-Specialized Multimodal Large Language Model for Road Distress Detection and Semantic Diagnostics
candidates.abstract: Objectives: Current automated road distress inspection systems are largely confined to visual localization and lack the semantic information needed for informed maintenance decisions. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown substantial potential in general scene understanding, their application to road distress is limited by domain misalignment and a shortage of high-quality, language-aligned datasets. The objective of this research is to develop RoadVerse, a domain-specialized MLLM that bridges visual distress localization with structured textual reasoning for road distress detection and semantic diagnostics. Methods: An automated multi-model collaborative framework synthesizes road distress images and generates paired bounding-box and natural-language annotations, resulting in the SRDD Benchmark. Eight representative open-source MLLMs are evaluated under zero-shot inference and supervised fine-tuning using Synthetic Road Distress Dataset (SRDD) and a manually annotated open-access dataset, with performance assessed in multi-label distress classification, localization and semantic description on four public road-distress datasets. Findings: Experiments on multiple public road-distress datasets show that SRDDbased adaptation consistently improves representative open-source MLLMs across classification, localization, and description tasks. These results demonstrate that structured generative multimodal data can provide effective supervision for domainspecific MLLM adaptation, achieving competitive or superior performance compared with manual-supervised settings. Novelty: This study presents an automated multi-model collaborative framework for constructing the language-aligned SRDD Benchmark. We develop RoadVerse as a unified domain-specialized MLLM for distress classification, localization, and maintenance-oriented semantic description. RoadVerse bridges visual distress localization with structured textual reasoning, extending detection-only pipelines toward integrated road distress detection and semantic diagnostics. Practical Applications: RoadVerse can support automated pavement inspection by converting road images into localized distress information and maintenance-relevant natural-language descriptions. These interpretable outputs can assist transportation practitioners with pavement-condition screening, maintenance prioritization, and followup inspection planning, while the data-generation framework reduces reliance on field collection and expert annotation.

candidates.title: Reasoning Across Relational Schemas with Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Relational databases underpin modern information systems, yet real-world data environments are increasingly heterogeneous, distributed, and fragmented across schemas with differing structures, naming conventions, and semantics. Although large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance in tasks such as Text-to-SQL generation and schema understanding, their ability to reason across multiple relational schemas remains poorly understood. This thesis investigates cross-schema relational reasoning in LLMs through three connected problems: cross-schema SQL query mapping, analysis of factors affecting mapping success, and schema reconstruction from fragmented databases. First, the thesis presents SQL-Exchange, a framework for transforming SQL queries across heterogeneous schemas while preserving source-query structure. Using schema-aware prompting, template-guided abstraction, and target-grounded value substitution, the framework enables structure-preserving query transfer across semantically different domains. Experiments show that LLMs can generate executable and semantically meaningful mappings, which further improve downstream Text-to-SQL performance, especially in low-resource settings. Second, the thesis analyzes why cross-schema SQL mappings succeed or fail. Using over 100,000 generated mappings, it examines the effects of query complexity, schema feasibility, and mapping flexibility on execution validity, semantic correctness, and structural preservation. Results indicate that complex query structures, schema incompatibilities, and ambiguous mappings significantly reduce performance, exposing key limitations of current LLMs under schema shift. Finally, the thesis studies whether LLMs can reconstruct coherent global schemas from fragmented local schemas in data integration scenarios. It introduces a benchmark for global schema construction based on real-world schemas subjected to controlled transformations, including naming drift, schema fragmentation, and removal of cross-source foreign keys. A deterministic evaluation framework measures executability, attribute recovery, and data reconstruction quality. Results show that even state-of-the-art reasoning LLMs struggle to recover globally consistent relational structures under high ambiguity and limited relational visibility. Overall, this thesis advances the study of schema-level reasoning in LLMs by introducing new methods, analyses, and benchmarks for relational reasoning across heterogeneous databases. The findings reveal both the promise and current limitations of LLMs in understanding, transferring, and reconstructing relational structure.

candidates.title: A Review of Video Large Language Models: From Spatiotemporal Representations to Reliable Reasoning
candidates.abstract: Video large language models connect video observations with user needs through natural language, allowing summarization, event localization, question answering, and ongoing interaction to draw on shared model capabilities. Yet accepting more frames or generating longer answers does not establish that a system has retained and correctly used the information required by a task. This review examines video understanding since the emergence of large language models, starting from application needs and proceeding through visual interfaces and representations, information management for long videos, intermediate reasoning, data and training, and capability validation. We first compare the pathways through which visual information enters a language model and examine how temporal computation and learning objectives jointly determine the distinctions a model can make. We then trace observation, compression, storage, and retrieval to explain how efficiency methods make decisions, where they save computation, and under what conditions omitted information can be recovered. On this basis, we distinguish relational organization, active observation, and judgment revision as functions of video reasoning, and analyze the roles of text, spatiotemporal anchors, latent features, and tool operations. The analysis indicates that fine-grained capabilities require training examples and objectives that explicitly distinguish the relevant changes; efficiency on long videos requires attention to both information retention and subsequent access; and the value of additional reasoning should be measured by the specific errors it corrects. We connect these findings to sample organization, parameter updates, process feedback, and diagnostic experiments, and discuss the conditions under which predictive and language learning, persistent memory, and transfer to generation and action can be effective. The resulting analysis supports technical choices under specific task requirements. Project repository: https://github.com/LeslieZhoa/Awesome_Video_Large_Language_Models

candidates.title: SchedOps-Bench and Vardiya: a live benchmark and an open harness for language-model agents in batch job scheduler operations
candidates.abstract: Batch job schedulers run the nightly file transfers, scripts and database loads of many organisations, and their administrators spend much of their time on routine repairs: a rotated password, a broken key permission, a held lock, a full disk, a wrong date pattern in a file name. I present SchedOps-Bench, a live benchmark in which a language-model agent acts as the scheduler administrator in a Docker lab with a real scheduler (JS7), two Linux agent hosts, an SFTP server and a PostgreSQL database. Each scenario really breaks the site, gives the agent a ticket that does not name the root cause, and judges the episode only by the end state read from the servers, with separate verdicts for partial, false green and harmful outcomes. The benchmark has 165 scenarios in six sets, each validated in both directions. I also present Vardiya, an open harness that aims to help small and mid-sized models adapt to this work, and compare three rungs: a bare model (zero by construction), a tool-equipped model with only the access layer, and Usta, the same model inside the full harness. The main measured gain is access: with tools, a light hosted model solves 15 of 15 development episodes. The harness adds step efficiency (8.3 against 14.1 steps on average) and, with a weaker model on the hidden test set, 11 of 27 against 8 of 26 correct with 1 against 4 harmful outcomes, a difference that is not statistically significant. With a small local model (qwen3:14b) on the development set, which the harness was tuned on, the harness removed all harmful outcomes (0 against 10 of 16) and raised correct episodes from 3 to 9. On the hard tier there is no correctness gain: on the 17-scenario hard hidden test set both arms are correct in 0 episodes. I release the lab, scenarios, harness, raw episode evidence and analysis scripts under Apache 2.0, and I present the hard tier as an open challenge.

candidates.title: Small language models are agentic but not autonomous in greenhouse climate control
candidates.abstract: Agentic large language models (LLMs) are proposed for cyber-physical control, yet evidence on how reliably small open-weight models turn sensor context into actuator commands is scarce. We present a reproducible benchmark grounded in an operational ESP32-based greenhouse controller: ninety-six generated test cases run against the production tool schema and prompts, scored deterministically, with the controller’s rule-based fallback ported verbatim as baseline. Four quantized models (3–14 B) ran on a pinned llama.cpp stack in two locked environments two months apart (12,000 scored runs). Three findings dominate. Autonomous self-initiation is far less reliable than command execution: models executing 65–100% of chat commands fall to 0.4–64.6% when acting unprompted. Model rankings are environment-conditional: one environment favoured Qwen2.5-7B over the 14B (McNemar p = 0.016; cluster-robust GEE p = 0.084), the other decisively reversed it at identical seeds ( p < 0.001; 77.5% cross-environment agreement), requiring re-benchmarking on the deployment stack. The rule baseline matches the second-best model with the best refusal behaviour: the LLM’s measured value is language-mediated actuation, knowledge capture, and auditability, not superior regulation. Field telemetry and thermal replay show the hybrid controller running unattended through the growing season, rules holding the safety-critical floor. All instruments and both environments’ traces are released.

candidates.title: SCRIPT: Scalable Diffusion Policy with Multi-stage Training for Language-driven Physics-Based Humanoid Control
candidates.abstract: Controlling physics-based humanoids from natural-language instructions is a critical step toward general-purpose embodied agents. However, existing methods remain constrained by a tension between semantic expressiveness and physical feasibility, often failing to jointly achieve faithful instruction following, high-quality motion, and stable long-horizon control. We propose SCRIPT, a scalable diffusion policy with a multi-stage training framework for language-driven physics-based humanoid control. The core of SCRIPT is a Joint Action-State-Text Diffusion Transformer (JAST-DiT), which represents actions, physical states, and text as dedicated token streams and couples them through joint attention, enabling direct interaction between language semantics and control dynamics. To stabilize autoregressive control, we introduce a nonlinear history conditioning mechanism, which preserves the dense recent context and samples increasingly sparse cues from long-term history. Beyond supervised imitation pre-training, we propose a post-training stage, further improving the performance using Reinforcement Learning with Hybrid Rewards (RLHR). By injecting learnable noise into the flow-sampling process, RLHR effectively improves motion quality and instruction following within closed-loop simulations using hybrid physical feedback and text rewards. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate that SCRIPT outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods, with gains across text alignment, motion quality, and physical realism metrics. Furthermore, scaling studies on the 1200-hour MotionMillion dataset demonstrate consistent performance gains with model scaling, highlighting SCRIPT's robust scalability for large-scale pre-training. Our code will be publicly available for future research.

candidates.title: Precision vs. Pragmatics: Benchmarking Post-Training Quantization Trade-offs in Sovereign Korean Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: The rapid deployment of Sovereign Large Language Models (LLMs) in South Korea requires balancing high computational efficiency with strict preservation of linguistic pragmatics, particularly hierarchical honorifics (Jondaetmal) and cultural context. While 4-bit Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) significantly reduces memory footprints for edge deployment on Neural Processing Units (NPUs), its impact on culturally sensitive Korean generation remains underexplored. In this study, we empirically benchmark the memory efficiency and pragmatic fidelity of 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) quantization applied to a 2.8-billion-parameter Korean sovereign LLM (EEVE-Korean-Instruct-2.8B-v1.0) on an NVIDIA T4 GPU. Our results demonstrate that NF4 quantization reduces model memory footprint by 67.2% (from 5.64 GB in FP16 to 1.85 GB in INT4) while preserving grammatical honorific structure in formal workplace communication.

candidates.title: Cognitive Offloading with Large Language Model Agents in Cybersecurity Education: Perceived Burden and Engagement in a Single-Cohort Study with Ten-Year Institutional Context
candidates.abstract: Practice-oriented cybersecurity education often requires novice learners to build target web systems by hand before security analysis begins, imposing extraneous cognitive load. An earlier study introduced a Red/Blue teaming model in which a large language model (LLM) agent builds the target systems (vibe coding) under Human-on-the-Loop (HOTL) control, so that learners audit, attack, and defend. This single-cohort study examines learner-level evidence from the 2026 cohort (n = 34) of a university web-security course, set against institutional Course-Quality-Improvement (CQI) satisfaction records for nine of the ten academic years 2017–2026. Evidence comprised self-reported coding-effort logs (n = 25), single-item final-course survey measures (n = 27), and peer cross-evaluation scores (71 ratings). Logged total coding effort had a median of 3.8 h. In the final-course survey, 96% agreed implementation burden had decreased and 93% that deeper engagement in vulnerability analysis and defense design was possible (raw means 4.67 and 4.44 of 5; Wilcoxon p < 0.001). The 2026 CQI score (91.55) ranked second among the nine records (descriptive). In this single-institution context, delegating system construction to an LLM agent was associated with lower perceived implementation burden, greater reported security-analysis engagement, and high satisfaction; multi-site replication is required.

candidates.title: Proposed new words and collective identity in human and language model agent groups
candidates.abstract: Abstract Groups develop distinctive words even when ordinary expressions are sufficient. Such words can symbolize collective identity, and observational studies link language use to community attachment. We examined identity change in temporary groups of one human and four disclosed large language model (LLM) agents, comparing discussions with and without a neologism proposal across recruitment waves. We recruited 100 Japanese participants in two sequential waves; an agent proposed a new word only in the first wave. Mean collective identity change did not differ significantly between waves. Within the proposal wave, favorable ratings of the proposed word were associated with change in identity, but this association did not survive correction for multiple testing (adjusted $$p=0.229$$ ). The three-way interaction among recruitment wave, message count, and team impression had a nominal $$p=0.027$$ but did not survive correction (adjusted $$p=0.082$$ ). In a sensitivity analysis, the interaction was not significant after adjustment for midpoint identity (nominal $$p=0.078$$ ; adjusted $$p=0.624$$ ). The nonsignificant between-wave comparison and exploratory associations that did not survive correction, together with wave confounding and post-discussion evaluations, limit causal inference and motivate randomized studies with repeated measures to test whether proposed group language affects identification.

candidates.title: Kompass: An Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation System for Personalized German University Admissions
candidates.abstract: The German higher education system offers tuition-free, world-class education, yet Indian students face a labyrinth of bureaucratic complexity—including the APS certificate, Uni-Assist, Blocked Accounts, and Anabin degree recognition—that is poorly served by generic Large Language Models. This paper presents Kompass, a public-facing Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system designed as an expert advisor for German admissions. Kompass employs a Hybrid Database Architecture (relational SQL + pgvector) to ground its responses in 6,000+ university programs and 100+ verified policy documents. A deterministic ”Pre-Flight Execution” router classifies user queries and invokes specialized Python tools for math, SQL filtering, OCR-based document parsing, and live web search, eliminating LLM hallucinations. Evaluation under adversarial testing demonstrates a 0% hallucination rate on fabricated universities and a 0% UI crash rate under API stress, with end-to-end response latency under 3.5 seconds. This work serves as a proof-of-concept for low-cost, domain-specific Agentic RAG systems across sectors. candidates.title: Theory of mind inspired mental state reasoning with large language models for empathetic response generation
candidates.abstract: Abstract As conversational AI expands into emotionally sensitive domains such as mental health support and counseling, empathetic response generation has become a key research challenge. Existing empathetic dialogue systems either reflect the user’s surface level emotions or, when relying on external commonsense knowledge bases, capture only generic patterns. We propose a Theory of Mind inspired framework in which a large language model first infers the speaker’s five mental states of Belief, Desire, Emotion, Intent, and Knowledge from the multi turn dialogue history and then uses them as conditioning signals for empathetic response generation. A preliminary study on a theory of mind benchmark indicates that the LLMs employed perform reasonably on mental state inference in both multiple choice and free form settings. On an empathetic dialogue dataset, injecting the self generated inferences improved response quality under both automatic metrics and LLM as judge evaluation. In the LoRA fine-tuned setting, the ToM condition performed comparably to COMET, an external commonsense knowledge baseline, with higher ROUGE-L point estimates for all four backbones and a significant advantage for one. Shuffled and corrupted descriptions consistently degraded response quality, whereas the ToM condition and a context-grounded factual-summary control performed similarly, indicating that contextual grounding is the primary source of the benefit. These findings suggest that speaker grounded mental state reasoning can be an effective strategy for empathetic dialogue systems.

candidates.title: Sniffing Large Language Models Over the Air
candidates.abstract: 1. Introduction TokenSniffer is an offline research pipeline for analyzing encrypted network traffic associated with large language model (LLM) interactions. It uses observable frame metadata to address three tasks, from detecting LLM usage to identifying the model deployment and recognizing the type of task being performed. LLM Usage Detection uses a LightGBM classifier to distinguish LLM traffic from ordinary application traffic. The training and evaluation scripts support fixed data splits and report test accuracy and macro-F1. Deployment Classifieridentifies the provider–model deployment associated with an LLM interaction. It uses a multiscale gated temporal convolutional network with masked attention pooling to classify sequences based on patterns across frames. Deployment-Specific Task Recognition trains a separate classifier for each model deployment. Each classifier predicts one of eight task categories, including writing, reasoning, mathematics, and coding. The training objective combines cross-entropy with weighted supervised contrastive learning to account for the relationship between augmented views of the same capture and examples from different captures. 2. Key Features Consistent traffic representation. All three stages use prepared sequences with 1,024 frame positions. Frame direction, normalized absolute frame length, and standardized log inter-frame arrival time are represented as separate input channels. Longer sequences are truncated and shorter sequences are padded with zeros. Normalization statistics are estimated from the training split and reused for validation and testing. Traffic sequence augmentation. The task recognition component supports timing jitter, frame dropout, and subsequence sliding. Training uses the original sample and its augmented views. The contrastive objective assigns each positive example from the same capture four times the weight of a positive example from a different capture before normalization. Training and evaluation with fixed splits. The included configurations and README commands support training with seeds 42–46. The neural classifiers select checkpoints using validation macro-F1 and evaluate those checkpoints on the held-out test split. Separate run directories make it possible to retain the outputs for each seed. 3. Package Contents TokenSniffer_source.zip contains the following files and directories under code/. llm_detection/ contains the LightGBM detector, frame preprocessing, data splitting, training, evaluation, and repeated-run scripts. deployment_classifier/ contains the deployment classifier, its training configuration, and entry points for preparing data, training, and prediction. task_recognition/ contains the task recognizer, augmentation methods, weighted contrastive loss, and training configurations for nine deployments. requirements.txt in each component lists the Python dependencies for that component. README.md documents the input format, task labels, expected directory structure, and commands for training and evaluation. 4. Basic Usage Extract the archive and create a Python 3.10 or later environment. Install the dependencies for the component you plan to run using its requirements.txt. Prepare the labeled JSONL records as described in the README. Each record contains aligned arrays for signed frame lengths and inter-frame arrival times. Use a fixed split manifest for LLM usage detection and separate training, validation, and test files for the neural classifiers. Run the training command for the selected component. For deployment classification and task recognition, set PYTHONPATH to that component’s src/ directory before running its training or prediction entry point.

candidates.title: Semantic-aware multimodal evidence integration with a lightweight large language model for rolling bearing fault diagnosis
candidates.abstract: Abstract Rolling bearings are critical components in industrial rotating machinery, and their failures may cause unexpected downtime, economic loss, and safety risks. Although deep learning and multimodal fusion have improved vibration-based fault diagnosis, two issues remain insufficiently addressed: magnitude-dominated time-frequency representations may discard phase-related impulse timing information, and heterogeneous diagnostic cues are often fused without explicit alignment in a semantically consistent representation space. This paper proposes M2-LLM-FD, a lightweight large language model-assisted framework for semantic-aware multimodal evidence integration in rolling bearing fault diagnosis. The framework converts each vibration segment into three complementary forms: time-domain patch tokens, phase-aware time-frequency tokens, and structured statistical prompts. A phase-preserving complex convolutional dimensionality reduction network is designed to process the real and imaginary components of the time-frequency representations, thereby retaining phase-sensitive information associated with fault-induced impulsive events. A structured multimodal alignment and fusion module then harmonizes temporal granularity and projects the aligned evidence into the pretrained language-model embedding space through semantic-anchor cross-modal attention. Furthermore, domain-specific prior knowledge is injected via structured statistical prompts, and the model is efficiently fine-tuned using Low-Rank Adaptation. \textcolor{red}{Extensive experiments on the CWRU, PU, and HUST datasets show that the proposed framework achieves consistent improvements in diagnostic accuracy, robustness, and cross-dataset generalization. Ablation and controlled analyses further validate the contributions of phase-aware time-frequency modeling, structured statistical prompts, and semantic-aware multimodal alignment to the overall diagnostic performance. The results indicate that combining phase-aware signal representation with large language model-compatible contextual evidence integration can effectively improve the robustness and generalization capability of intelligent bearing fault diagnosis.

candidates.title: On the Use of Large Language Models for Inter-Model Consistency Specification
candidates.abstract: Cyber-physical systems are developed using heterogeneous modeling frameworks that address different engineering concerns and abstraction levels. In practice, models from mechanical, electrical, and software engineering coexist across development phases, creating the need to specify inter-model consistency despite differences in terminology, structure, and execution semantics. A first step of such a specification is to identify which modeling constructs of two frameworks correspond, that is, whose instances have to be kept consistent, and along which dimensions. In this paper, we investigate how well Large Language Models (LLMs) perform this correspondence identification for pairs of modeling constructs, compared with expert references. We use two gold-standard datasets: 90 automotive construct pairs across AUTOSAR, ROS 2, CAD, Simulink, and a brake specification metamodel, annotated by three experts, and 32 smart-grid construct pairs across three IEC metamodels, whose reference labels are derived from a published rule-based integration. Each pair is labeled on an ordinal scale along three dimensions: syntactic, semantic, and behavioral. Six large language models from OpenAI and Google are evaluated under zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot prompting, together with two agentic systems, OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code, run with web access allowed or disabled. We report Quadratic Weighted Kappa, Mean Absolute Error, accuracy, and macro-F1 with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests. On average, the LLMs agree with the references beyond chance and beyond string- and embedding-based baselines, but ordinal agreement remains weak to moderate. On the automotive pairs with traceable independent annotations, the agreement of the best configurations with individual experts does not differ significantly from the agreement among the experts, whereas most configurations agree less in the semantic dimension and, on the AUTOSAR–ROS 2 pairs, also in the syntactic dimension. Over both datasets, semantic correspondence is judged more reliably than syntactic correspondence. Vendor differences are small and dimension-specific, and in-context examples improve agreement only in selected dimensions. On the automotive pairs, the ordinal agreement of the agentic systems does not exceed that of the best direct configurations. On the smart-grid pairs, for which their prompts, unlike the direct prompts, define the dimensions in the terms used to derive the reference labels, they reach higher syntactic agreement. Web access does not improve their agreement consistently. Overall, LLMs can support experts in identifying correspondences, but they do not replace expert judgment.

candidates.title: Large Language Model Classification Validation Matching Task
candidates.abstract: Textual data can be grouped and classified with various methods. These include classical topic models such as latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) and newer approaches based on text embeddings, such as BERTopic. We present a method that clusters embeddings in a way similar to the BERTopic workflow, but uses a large language model (LLM) for the final classification. Because classifications by an LLM are not fully reproducible, as repeated runs can assign a statement to different categories, we test whether human raters arrive at the same classification. To validate the LLM classification, we test whether human raters assign statements on 1) drivers of psychosocial risks, 2) solution ideas, and 3) derived interventions to the same categories as the LLM.

candidates.title: Instrumenting Failure: Scoring Language Model Agents at Every Decision Node in Imperfect-Information Games
candidates.abstract: Agent evaluations report task success and rarely say what an agent did at each decision. We score every decision node of three 12B to 14B instruct-tuned language models (LMs) playing five zero-sum imperfect-information games against four opponents on eight properties from decision and game theory, five of them against a CFR+ equilibrium reference. At each node, the LM also states a belief about the opponent's hidden state in a separate call. Without memory and at temperature 0, stated beliefs sit 0.250 to 0.288 in total variation distance from the equilibrium posterior, and where the action responds to the state its agreement with that belief exceeds chance by -0.04 to 0.19. The two calls frame the opponent differently, so the result is a behavioural inconsistency and makes no claim about internal beliefs. Under one prompt and greedy decoding, the LM's action never varies with the state in 10 of the 38 cells where the reference varies its own. Memory lowers the constant-action share in 9 of 13 testable ladders at temperature 0; at temperature 0.2 the cells at 1 fall from 16 to 5 of the 46 informative cells, while the belief results hold. A gate withholds, with a stated reason, any belief score the run cannot support, and seven of the eight non-zero defect rates are attributable to the instrument, a representation, or the LMs.

candidates.title: A Context-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework for Personalized Learning and Automated Course Development
candidates.abstract: The rapid growth of digital learning resources has created both opportunity and overload for learners navigating online education. This paper presents EDURAG, an AI-powered personalized learning and course generation platform that combines generative artificial intelligence with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to deliver adaptive, context-aware educational experiences. EDURAG integrates secure user authentication, a personalized analytics dashboard, automated course generation, structured lesson management, progress tracking, and a conversational AI teacher grounded in a curated knowledge base. The platform is built on a modern full-stack architecture using Next.js, React, and Tailwind CSS on the client and application layer, with Prisma ORM and SQLite for structured data persistence, and JWT/Jose-based authentication secured by bcrypt password hashing. This paper describes the motivation, system architecture, implementation, and functional modules of EDURAG, and situates the platform within the broader literature on intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning, and retrieval-augmented generation. We discuss how the fusion of generative and retrieval-based methods mitigates hallucination and improves factual grounding in AI tutoring responses, while also examining limitations such as data quality dependency, domain coverage, and the ethical considerations inherent in AI-mediated education. The paper concludes that EDURAG demonstrates a practical, extensible architecture for trustworthy, personalized AI-driven learning and outlines directions for future research and development.

candidates.title: Language-model agents' beliefs can be manipulated via truthful evidence in open channel
candidates.abstract: Language-model agents' beliefs can be manipulated through open channels such as social media, even when the information they receive is truthful. When agents fill gaps between fragments with self-induced relationships, they may accept those relationships as established facts and pass the resulting rumours to others. Drawing on cognitive theory of narrative understanding and film theory of montage, we introduce Generative Montage to operationalize this failure, termed narrative overfitting, by coordinating agents to arrange truthful fragments into misleading narratives. Across 1,090 rumour targets from six Twitter events, agents often accepted rumours overconfidently, with overall acceptance exceeding 65 percent in twelve of fourteen models. Acceptance remained above 50 percent after majority voting or review of the same evidence, showing how errors can reach downstream decisions. To explain this susceptibility, fragment interventions identify posts that influence belief within complete narratives. Synthetic controls then show that similar response patterns arise from valid evidence, separating belief influence from evidential support. This distinction motivates Grounded Monitor, a proof-of-concept neuro-symbolic runtime monitor that checks direct evidential support to guide agents' judgements, improving decision accuracy by 5.6 to 29.0 percentage points across original and anonymized settings. These findings expose a cognitive route to rumour amplification and support monitoring inferred relationships before agent-generated conclusions guide public decisions.

candidates.title: Idempotency Is Not Recovery: A Fault-Injection Study of Language-Model Agent Tool Actions
candidates.abstract: When a language-model agent's tool call is interrupted, the action may already have changed an external system without confirmation. Retrying risks duplication; assuming success may conceal an action that never occurred. We study these failure modes in a controlled agent runtime combining authorization, an action ledger, target-side idempotency, reconciliation, and evidence sealing. We inject ten single-host fault classes and compare four configurations and three ablations using a target-side oracle separate from the runtime ledger. On each of Windows and Linux, 7,513 trials used 96 captured model responses from 24 constructed cases. In 200 known original crash and replay pairs, the full configuration recorded 0/200 repeated effects versus 117/200 for each simpler baseline. A ledger-related ablation had 170/170 orphaned effects versus 0/170 and 200/300 recovery successes versus 300/300 for the full configuration. Disabling reconciliation left 100/100 known post-effect crash outcomes ambiguous despite no observed duplicates. A separate supplement designed after the initial results and reusing the same inputs found a similar pattern under response loss or delay. The full runtime had about one-seventh of fail-open throughput, while injected evidence-write faults left 75/100 trials per platform unresolved. These findings distinguish duplicate suppression from recovery and identify their measured reliability and performance tradeoffs within the tested benchmark.

candidates.title: Disaggregated LLM Inference in Space: A Communication Feasibility Study
candidates.abstract: Orbital data centers could enable large-scale AI inference, but efficiently serving a frontier language model to many users may require several compute satellites to cooperate over optical links. While disaggregated inference, which splits large language model (LLM) serving across machines, is well established in terrestrial data centers, its viability under the unique constraints of orbital deployments remains an open question. This article investigates how link capacity and satellite separation affect two types of disaggregated LLM serving, in both compact satellite formations and distributed constellations. Prefill-decode disaggregation (PDD) migrates a large KV cache once per request, while attention-FFN disaggregation (AFD) exchanges small activations at every mixture-of-experts layer for every generated token. The two respond to distance in different ways. PDD is limited mainly by link capacity and, with fast enough links, tolerates separations of up to a thousand kilometers. AFD is limited mainly by propagation delay, which accumulates layer by layer and forces attention and expert instances within about a kilometer of each other. Based on these results, we propose a hierarchical orbital inference architecture and provide network design guidelines for future orbital data centers, including the role of ground access latency.

candidates.title: Conclusion and Roadmap for AI and LLM
candidates.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) in the healthcare sector, educational infrastructure, legal analytics, and the academic publishing field has reshaped these sectors. Utilizing such architecture with transformers, LLMs show extraordinary performance due to their natural language comprehension and their ability to reason within context and generate textual material. There are, however, frequent problems in the deployment, such as mitigation of bias, interpretability, computational efficiency, and ethical governance. In the chapter, the results of studies in peer-reviewed journals are generalized; theories and practical limitations are critically appraised; and the specific application of the domain in such fields as cardiology, ophthalmology, education, and legal technology is discussed. It also discusses novel hybrid systems based on combining LLMs with knowledge graphs (KGs) as a solution to more factually grounded and less hallucinatory systems. The suggested framework combines modular design, a well-organized workflow pipeline, and human feedback cycles to be more flexible and reliable. The comparisons of performance in various areas demonstrate that LLMs with KG hybrids are particularly more accurate when comparing facts than the standard LLMs, but with a slight disadvantage in inference time software. The chapter culminates with a multi-stage plan of the future work, providing short-, mid-, and long-term plans with regard to domain adaptation, ethical AI models, and energy-efficient model design.

candidates.title: Case Studies in AI and LLM Integration
candidates.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems grow in scale, efficiency, and sophistication, future trends indicate a shift towards more human-like understanding, multimodal capabilities (integrating text, images, audio, and video), and real-time reasoning. The integration of large language models (LLMs) with edge computing, cloud infrastructure, and specialized hardware (such as AI accelerators) will enhance deployment efficiency and reduce latency. Furthermore, responsible AI practices—such as transparency, fairness, privacy preservation, and energy-efficient architectures—are gaining importance. Federated learning, fine-tuning with smaller datasets, and domain-specific customization are expected to make LLMs more accessible and practical across industries. As the boundaries between symbolic reasoning and neural networks blur, we anticipate the emergence of hybrid models capable of both statistical learning and logical inference. These trends will define the next generation of intelligent systems, enabling more adaptive, context-aware, and ethically grounded applications in healthcare, education, governance, and beyond.

candidates.title: Interactive Structured Environment Scaling for Large Language Model Agentic Reasoning
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning via environmental interaction is a cornerstone post-training paradigm for evolving large language models into autonomous agents capable of multi-turn tool use and exploration. Because the environment defines what the policy observes and how actions are verified, its structure directly bounds the capabilities an agent can acquire. Yet existing structured and retrieval environments rely on upstream pre-filtering---extracting a compact subgraph around the gold answer or retrieving fixed passages before the policy acts. We show that such pre-filtering introduces a fundamental measurement confound: because per-question subgraphs enclose ground-truth paths, they compress the candidate space by orders of magnitude and leak answer locations via local topology, allowing a question-blind degree heuristic to surface gold answers far above chance. To restore path selection, candidate pruning, and optimal stopping as genuine policy decisions, we propose RISE (Interactive Structured Environment), which transitions structured reinforcement learning from static subgraphs to full-scale interactive databases along two coupled axes. First, Decision-Space Scaling exposes the unpruned knowledge graph via a five-stage graph-agnostic typed intent adapter under a bounded call budget and a multiplicative grounding reward gate. Second, Learning-Frontier Scaling overcomes within-group variance collapse under group-normalized objectives by uniting model-independent structural tier progression with a self-evolving competence-frontier bandit. Across nineteen benchmarks and three model backbones, RISE substantially advances in-domain and unseen-schema knowledge-graph reasoning, transfers zero-shot to open-domain passage retrieval, and significantly enhances out-of-domain mathematical and logical deduction.

candidates.title: Shift records and gallery for the article "Large language model agents as operators of an exothermic chemical reactor"
candidates.abstract: This package accompanies the article "Large language model agents as operators of an exothermic chemical reactor" by T. Sainio, N. Groll, and G. Sin. It contains the machine-readable records of all 1224 reactor-operation episodes (shifts) of the article, a gallery of static HTML pages for browsing them, and every text that the agents received. In every shift, a large language model (LLM) agent operated a simulated non-isothermal continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) with three steady states and a high-temperature interlock, in real time, through a tool interface. The outcome of each shift was scored from the true state of the simulated plant. The LLMs were Claude Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 (Anthropic). Each shift record gives the design labels, the true plant trajectory at 1 s resolution, the measurements returned to the agent, every tool call made by the agent, every input change, the alarm and interlock events, the token counts of every call to the LLM, the scored outcome, the quantities that the article derives from the shift, and the text that the agent wrote (its messages during the shift, the reasons given with its forecasts, its debrief and its answers to the questions asked outside the shifts). Three CSV tables list the shifts, the ignitions and the cases. The package does not contain the agents' reasoning summaries or the session logs of the agent tool. To browse the shifts, unpack the archive and open index.html in a web browser. Nothing needs to be installed. README.md describes every file and field, and checksums.sha256 gives the SHA-256 of every file.

candidates.title: Ablation study of correction methods in Polish language Retrieval-Augmented Generation chatbots
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates hallucinations in large language models by grounding responses in retrieved evidence, yet the interplay of correction techniques across the RAG pipeline remains underexplored – especially for non-English languages. We present a modular RAG system evaluated through a systematic ablation study of 12 pipeline configurations on a 1,000-question Polish-language test set derived from a 1M-article Wikipedia corpus and manually validated. Four correction families are compared: (i) cross- -encoder reranking, (ii) query decomposition with multi-hop reranking and diversity enforcement, (iii) native Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, and (iv) post-generative Chain-of-Verification (CoVe). Results evaluated with RAGAS metrics show that multi-hop reranking yields the largest quality gains (Δ Faithfulness +15.6%, Δ Context Recall +38.4%, Δ Relevancy +20.3%) at acceptable latency (18.4 s), while CoVe in auto-correction mode can paradoxically degrade faithfulness at high computational cost (+41.6 s). Cross-encoder reranking achieves the best cost quality ratio (+16.7% Recall, +1.2 s). We discuss practical configuration tiers for real- -time, interactive, and offline deployments.

candidates.title: FRAAC: A French Multimodal Large Language Model and Dataset forPictogram-Based Augmentative and Alternative Communication
candidates.abstract: Pictograms are a core modality in augmentative and alternative communication (AAC), yet recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) cannot reliably interpret or produce pictogram sequences. Two obstacles explain this gap: the absence of a standardized pictogram grammar and the scarcity of parallel text-pictogram data. We introduce Retrieval-Augmented Pictogram Selection (RAPS), an annotation method that refines a rule-based transcription system's output with LLM-based concept extraction and retrieval over a pictogram vocabulary, handling cases where hand-written rules fail (named entities, numbers, polysemous words) without requiring new rules. Applied to French, RAPS yields a synthetic corpus of 1.4 million parallel pairs, of which 300k are publicly released. In a human ranking study where annotators order four pictogram transcriptions of the same sentence, RAPS outperforms the rule-based state of the art. Moreover, we show that standard reference-based metrics separate systems of clearly different quality but fail to rank strong systems against each other. Finally, we build an instruction-tuned model that supports interaction in several AAC modalities: it accepts pictogram or text input and answers in pictograms, speech, or text.

candidates.title: Large language model agent simulations of individual differences in social interactions
candidates.abstract: A key challenge in the behavioral sciences is the lack of formal models that capture individual differences in social interactions. At the same time, recent advances in artificial intelligence offer new opportunities to simulate and assess interpersonal behavior at scale. In this study, we introduce an agent-based modeling framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to simulate short-term social interactions. Within a dyadic interaction cycle, an LLM-based agent continually adjusts its interpersonal behavior (agency and communion) to its prior behavior, the partner’s behavior, and the combined influence of behavioral defaults (differences in default behavioral tendencies) and interpersonal reactivities (differences in reactions to partner behaviors). We derive a mathematical model that formalizes how interpersonal behavior unfolds across the interaction, evaluate the model in simulations, illustrate how the framework expresses these interpersonal dynamics in natural language, and outline the framework’s flexibility for simulating individual differences in practical applications across the behavioral sciences.

candidates.title: Adversarial Post-Training of Foundation Models for High-Frequency Trading
candidates.abstract: While autoregressive foundation models trained on limit order book (LOB) data show state-of-the-art performance for market simulation, pre-training with cross-entropy neither penalizes the compounding of sampling errors over free-running rollouts nor targets desired market properties. We introduce a post-training method for LOB foundation models using a Wasserstein generative adversarial network (GAN) objective. A critic, trained online on rollouts through the true, non-differentiable matching engine, guides updates from evolution strategies over rank-4 LoRA perturbations of the pre-trained generator, under a KL trust region. For efficiency, we use EGGROLL (Evolution Guided GeneRal Optimisation via Low-rank Learning), a memory-efficient variant of evolution strategies. On a held-out panel, adversarial post-training improves LOB-Bench realism by \(17.6\%\) (WS-21) and \(17.0\%\) (Mean-L1), while selection-matched random-perturbation and compute-matched continued-pre-training controls yield no improvement. Post-training is thus a necessary stage that more pre-training does not replace. Per-position divergence measurements show that it slows error accumulation over 500-message rollouts from 3.1 × to 2.3 ×. Adversarial post-training is also inexpensive, requiring under 50 M training tokens and 12 GPU-hours per seed, three orders of magnitude below the 48 B-token pre-training budget. Ablations over critic inputs, optimizers, and the population–rollout trade-off, together with an analysis of reward hacking, yield practical design guidelines for adversarial post-training.

candidates.title: Vision language model (VLM)-enabled counterfactual reasoning for illegal dumping profiling in metropolitan cities
candidates.abstract: Street view analytics (SVA) has gained increasing value in environmental criminology. However, most of the analyses are based only on limited factual information, which could lead to potential bias and limit opportunities to investigate the effect of a specific factor of interest while holding others constant. Generating counterfactual street views using vision language models (VLMs) provides a promising avenue for counterfactual reasoning and allows for the controlled study of individual factors. This study presents a novel approach that generates diverse counterfactual street views and compares them with their factual counterparts, using illegal dumping sites in urban environments as a case study. The baseline is a dataset of 757 Google Street Views (GSVs), of which 506 are illegal dumping sites and 251 are controls. Seven VLMs were benchmarked, and Nano Banana Pro was chosen to generate 1000 more counterfactual views with different featured factors. Of these, 921 passed quality screening and were retained for the main analysis. The data was analyzed by two high-powered VLMs namely GPT-5.5 and Claude Sonnet 4.6. In both evaluator graphs, visible litter and surface defects were associated with higher model scores for identifying illegal dumping sites, and well-maintained pavement with lower scores. The resulting graphs describe responses to controlled visual edits and provide hypotheses about environmental influences for future field validation. This approach can be scaled to broader studies of location-based environmental crime.

candidates.title: Rocks, Pebbles and Sand: Modality-aware Scheduling for Multimodal Large Language Model Inference
candidates.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) power platforms like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot, enabling rich interactions across text, images, and videos. Unlike text-only workloads, multimodal requests are inherently heterogeneous, differing by orders of magnitude in latency and memory footprint. Existing LLM serving systems, designed for homogeneous text workloads, struggle under this heterogeneity: large image and video requests monopolize GPU resources, causing severe head-of-line blocking and degrading the responsiveness of lightweight, latency-critical text queries. Recent multimodal serving systems mitigate this interference through disaggregation, isolating encoding and inference stages across GPUs. While effective at large scale, such designs introduce severe GPU underutilization in more practical, moderate-scale deployments. In response, we build RPS-Serve a modality-aware scheduling framework that leverages the extreme heterogeneity in multimodal workloads and introduces a simple abstraction: videos behave like rocks, images like pebbles, and text like sand. Then, it lets sand flow quickly through pebbles and rocks, maximizing GPU utilization while ensuring fast responsiveness for lightweight requests and controlled execution for heavier ones. To achieve this, RPS-Serve estimates the GPU admission cost of each request, classifies requests into rocks, pebbles, and sand using lightweight clustering, and applies priority-based scheduling with aging to balance performance across modalities. Evaluation across state-of-the-art MLLMs shows that RPS-Serve increases GPU utilization by 65% and reduces TTFT by up to 9.3 ×, on average across models, compared to disaggregation-based multimodal systems.
