candidates.title: Primitives and Paths: Predicting What Post-Training Can Do from What the Base Model Already Has
candidates.abstract: Does reinforcement learning teach language models new capabilities, or merely amplify ones acquired during pre-training? The literature offers evidence for both: pass@$k$ studies suggest RL reweights latent behaviours while some controlled composition studies demonstrate gains beyond simple amplification. We argue that this question has no answer independent of the capability state of the base model, and propose a two-dimensional state space for post-trainability. The first axis, \(\emph{effective full-solution support}\), measures whether successful trajectories can be sampled under a feasible exploration budget. The second axis, \(\emph{atomic primitive coverage}\), measures whether the constituent skills of a solution can be executed when the burden of composition is removed. Together, these dimensions motivate three regimes -- amplification, composition-limited, and acquisition-limited -- each predicting a distinct empirical signature and calling for a distinct intervention. We propose a prospective measurement protocol and investigate the framework using synthetic composition tasks across three small language models. We find that primitive mastery alone does not guarantee that RL can learn a composition. Checkpoints that execute every primitive reliably can fail to improve when complete solutions are never sampled during training, whereas modest composition supervision that establishes nonzero support enables substantial RL gains. The framework reframes mid-training as preparation for post-training: its role is to move models into states from which RL can operate effectively.

candidates.title: Large Language Models for AI Infrastructure
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to design, optimize, and operate the infrastructure behind AI training and serving, yet the literature remains fragmented across hardware design, machine learning systems, electronic design automation, and high-performance computing. We present a comprehensive survey of LLM-assisted AI infrastructure across its lifecycle, from accelerator design and kernel engineering to compilation, deployment, operations, data management, and energy optimization. We organize the literature by the primary resource the LLM manages: artifact-centric methods for computational artifacts, operational-centric methods for deployment context and system state, and resource-centric methods for data and energy. These categories span the lifecycle and cover AI-specific concerns such as distributed-training configuration, inference serving, GPU-cluster scheduling, and data loading. Building on this taxonomy, we conduct a cross-study quantitative synthesis of reported results. Because studies adopt heterogeneous benchmarks, baselines, hardware, and metrics, we compare methods only where evaluation conditions permit and align results along common dimensions: functional correctness, execution performance, throughput, resource and energy consumption, operational outcomes, and optimization cost, keeping each result's native metric, baseline, and setting rather than collapsing them into a single score. This comparison reveals where LLM-driven methods yield consistent gains, how reported gains in workload orchestration depend on the evaluation environment, from simulators to real clusters and production, and where evidence is still lacking. Together, the taxonomy, lifecycle perspective, and quantitative evaluation provide an evidence-grounded reference for LLM-driven engineering of AI infrastructure.

candidates.title: Beyond Paired Inputs: Learning to Leverage RGB-T Cross-Modal Relations in Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: RGB and thermal infrared (TIR) sensors provide complementary observations, yet their distinct sensing characteristics make effective cross-modal coordination challenging. Although existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can process paired RGB-T inputs, they often fail to translate cross-modal relations into effective task-specific decisions, leaving the potential of these relations to improve task performance and robustness largely untapped. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RelMLLM, an RGB-T MLLM that explicitly learns to exploit cross-modal relations in task-specific decision making. It represents modality reliability, the cross-modal relation, and the dominant modality as a verifiable decision state. We derive task-grounded supervision for this state by comparing RGB-only, TIR-only, and paired RGB-T task outcomes. A hierarchical relation-guided reward supervises modality-specific evidence, relation-state prediction, and the final task output, while encouraging consistency across evidence, relation, and decision. We evaluate RelMLLM on natural RGB-T grounding, RGB-T visual question answering, and held-out sensor degradation. RelMLLM improves grounding accuracy and degradation robustness over its Qwen3-VL baselines while preserving performance on general RGB-T reasoning benchmarks. These results demonstrate that effectively exploiting cross-modal relations leads to more accurate and robust RGB-T decisions. Code and model weights are publicly available.

candidates.title: JetFire: Approximate-then-Correct Attention on Hybrid Memory for Long-Context LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which the key–value (KV) cache rapidly exhausts. Existing designs compress, select, or offload KV entries, exposing trade-offs among HBM use, approximation error, and data movement. Our key insight is that locating the few tokens that dominate attention needs far less precision than computing the output over them: a heavily quantized cache can no longer reproduce the output, yet it still ranks tokens reliably. JetFire exploits this asymmetry with an approximate-then-correct (ATC) attention backend over hybrid memory. A dense low-precision pipeline scans a compact replica of the whole sequence in GPU HBM, fitting long contexts without dropping tokens. A sparse high-precision pipeline on the CPU corrects the dominant tokens from the full-precision replica in host DRAM. The correction overlaps the GPU value phase when transfer and computation fit within it. JetFire remains near-lossless relative to full attention, and JetFire-K3V2 achieves 1.3–3.0 × speedup in end-to-end execution time over TurboQuant within vLLM at the largest common contexts. Against offloading-based systems, it achieves 1.4–2.7 × speedup over NEO and 13–180 × over InfiniGen. JetFire is open-sourced at https://github.com/Xtra-Computing/JetFire.

candidates.title: HeadFlow: Scaling Long-Context Training with Head-Group Activation Residency
candidates.abstract: Training generative models on long contexts is increasingly bottlenecked by attention activation GPU residency: activations must be on GPU when they are produced and later reused, yet keeping all of them resident limits context length. This paper presents HeadFlow , a runtime system that recasts attention activation management as a head-group lifetime planning problem. HeadFlow exploits a long-context asymmetry: attention compute grows rapidly with sequence length, while each head group’s activation state grows much more slowly, creating windows that can hide movement. It names semantic activation slots, places them across CPU pinned memory, direct GPU–SSD storage, staged GPU–CPU–SSD paths, or recomputation, and executes the resulting plan with asynchronous save, staged prefetch, and load. We implement HeadFlow by extending FlashAttention-compatible operators with plan-aware asynchronous activation movement, and evaluate it across long-context language and multimodal generative training. On text workloads, HeadFlow trains with 512K–1M-token contexts. Its throughput is 1.33 × –1.67 × that of state-of-the-art sequence- and context-parallel baselines. To our knowledge, HeadFlow is the first system to train a 24B model with full parameters at 1M context on only eight 96GB H20 GPUs. On image and video workloads, the same runtime extends the maximum trainable effective tokens by 4.0 × and achieves a 1.32 × speedup. Loss and attention-gradient checks confirm that these gains come from exact activation management rather than approximate attention or lossy execution.

candidates.title: Requests of a Feather Must Flock Together: Batch Size vs. Prefix Homogeneity in LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Auto-regressive token generation in large language models is memory-bound because it requires “attending to” key and value tensors (KV cache) of all previous tokens. Prior work aims to improve the efficiency of this decode process by batching multiple requests together, and maximizing batch size subject to GPU memory constraints. The key observation of our work is that with prefix-sharing workloads, smaller, prefix-homogeneous batches – where all requests share a common prefix – can achieve higher decode throughput than larger, heterogeneous batches, due to better spatial and temporal locality during KV cache accesses. However, current prefix-aware schedulers maximize prefix reuse within a batch only to reduce KV cache memory footprint, but do not stop batch formation at smaller homogeneous batches that could have performed better. Further, we show that shared prefix detection in existing schedulers relies on radix-tree traversals, incurring substantial CPU overhead that is often comparable to GPU execution time. This paper presents Feather , a prefix-aware scheduler that uses reinforcement learning (RL) to learn the optimal tradeoff between batch size and prefix homogeneity. We also introduce Chunked Hash Tree (CHT), a lightweight data structure that enables fast prefix detection and efficient request selection for the RL scheduler, avoiding expensive tree traversals. We integrate Feather into vLLM and SGLang, and our evaluation shows that Feather achieves 2–10 × higher end-to-end throughput as compared to existing schedulers by reducing the total number of KV cache accesses, while doing no worse than the status quo when there is insufficient prefix sharing.

candidates.title: RS-Infer: A Fast and Secure LLM Inference System for Mobile Devices with Recallable Resource Isolation
candidates.abstract: The adoption of device-side Large Language Models (LLMs) has grown rapidly, offering stronger privacy and higher availability than their cloud-side counterparts. Attackers may compromise the OS kernel to steal valuable model weights and user data. ARM TrustZone is the de facto hardware-based isolation technology on mobile devices, used to protect sensitive applications from a compromised OS. However, protecting LLM inference with TrustZone incurs significant overhead for both the secure inference and the normal applications, due to two challenges: the inflexible resource isolation and the inefficient secure resource management. To address these challenges, this paper presents RS-Infer, a fast and secure LLM inference system for mobile devices. The key idea is to decouple the access permission from the management permission of secure resources, so that the normal-world OS cannot access them but can still manage them as usual. First, RS-Infer introduces a Recallable Resource Isolation mechanism to construct Recallable Secure Memory (RS-Memory) and a Recallable Secure NPU (RS-NPU). They can only be accessed by the secure world, but can be efficiently allocated and reclaimed by the normal-world OS. Based on them, RS-Infer further introduces the RS-Infer Framework to run secure LLM inference in the secure world. It cooperates with the normal-world OS to manage secure memory. We evaluate an RS-Infer prototype against a TrustZone-based Strawman and its optimized variant. RS-Infer achieves average TTFT speedups of 8.00 × and 2.19 × , respectively, and average response latency speedups of 14.15 × and 2.94 × for multi-model agent workflows.

candidates.title: Model-as-a-Service in the Wild: Characterizing Production LLM Inference Clusters at Scale
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference has been widely deployed in modern cloud platforms as Model-as-a-Service (MaaS), serving both online and offline applications on shared, heterogeneous GPU clusters. Recent characterization studies have examined request-level workload patterns, but cluster-wide resource patterns and system-level deployment behaviors remain largely unexplored. This missing view is critical for diagnosing production bottlenecks and for understanding whether and how existing inference techniques should be applied in real MaaS systems. In this paper, we analyze a six-month production LLM inference trace from xMaaS , a large-scale MaaS platform with over 100K GPUs. xMaaS provides a detailed system view of cluster resources and their allocation across 300K applications and 70K model variants, enabling a resource-centric analysis across cluster, application, and model levels. Our study characterizes how heterogeneous GPU resources are supplied and utilized, how application resource demand is distributed and evolves over time, and how model variants and serving modes affect resource allocation on heterogeneous hardware. Based on these observations, we further analyze deployment implications and identify open problems for production MaaS systems, which we hope will motivate future research on resource-efficient LLM inference.

candidates.title: Can a Multi-Agentic Small Language Model framework Compete with a Single-Agent LLM in Portfolio Rebalancing?
candidates.abstract: Large language models can integrate heterogeneous financial evidence, but their cost, latency, and data-governance requirements can limit repeated portfolio-level inference. We evaluate whether a role-specialized multi-agent small language model system can provide a competitive alternative to a single-agent large language model for monthly portfolio rebalancing. The proposed system, SLM-Multi, instantiates Gemma 4 E4B across four specialized investment roles with selective debate. The comparator, LLM-Single, is Gemini 2.5 Flash operating as one consolidated agent. Both systems operate under a common downstream portfolio-construction pipeline, enabling a matched comparison of the two complete reasoning systems. We evaluate both systems across ten pre-specified six-stock portfolios and 15 monthly rebalances from January 2025 through March 2026. SLM-Multi achieved a mean net cumulative return of 18.28%, compared with 16.57% for LLM-Single, and a mean annualized Sharpe ratio of 0.757 versus 0.675. SLM-Multi achieved higher cumulative returns in all ten portfolios, lower average turnover, and a slightly shallower mean maximum drawdown. These results demonstrate that a structured multi-agent SLM system can achieve competitive portfolio-level performance relative to a consolidated LLM under a common portfolio-construction protocol.

candidates.title: From Large Language Models (LLMs) to Agentic AI for IoT Security: A Survey
candidates.abstract: Securing the Internet of Things (IoT) requires detecting and responding to evolving threats across distributed devices with limited computing and communication resources. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret security alerts and help investigate incidents. Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) extends these capabilities by combining reasoning, planning, memory, and tool use to coordinate security actions. Existing studies offer a fragmented account of how these capabilities fit IoT architectures, what risks arise when agents act autonomously, and how to evaluate their performance. This survey addresses these gaps by tracing the transition from LLM-assisted analysis to agentic defence across threat detection, triage, investigation, and response. We develop a unified taxonomy covering IoT infrastructure, LLM-driven and agentic security, trust and resilience, application domains, and evaluation methods. We compare hierarchical, orchestration-based, distributed multi-agent, and cognitive architectures by examining where security decisions are made, how agents coordinate, and where actions are executed across device, edge, fog, and cloud layers. We also examine threats introduced by agentic operation, including prompt injection, memory poisoning, privacy leakage, and compromised trust between agents, together with corresponding defences. Our synthesis finds that limited attack testing and dataset coverage leave uncertainty about how well these systems generalize, while coordination failures and inference overhead constrain deployment. These findings motivate research on trustworthy orchestration, privacy-preserving collaboration, explainable security decisions, and efficient edge inference.

candidates.title: Execution-Guided Verification for Reliable Tool-Using Large Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate on real systems through tool calls, yet their behavior is stochastic: the same request may be resolved correctly in one run and incorrectly in the next, and erroneous write operations are costly to undo. This paper presents execution-guided verification (EGV), a training-free and model-agnostic procedure that decides which agent behavior to commit by executing candidate trajectories instead of judging their text. EGV replays the tool calls of k independently sampled trajectories against isolated copies of the backend state, groups candidates that reach an identical final world state, and commits a representative of the best-supported state, while failed tool calls serve as a secondary signal for tie-breaking and representative selection. The support share of the committed state acts as a verification confidence for selective execution with escalation to human operators. Experiments on 1,980 real trajectories of GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet in the retail and airline domains of τ-bench, replayed in a sandbox that reproduces 99.96% of the recorded tool observations, show that EGV improves task success over single-run execution in every setting, e.g., from 61.0% to 68.7% for Claude-3.5-Sonnet in retail, with a pooled gain of 6.1 points (95% CI [3.8, 8.3]), and that it consistently outperforms voting over emitted action sequences. Execution agreement predicts trajectory success with an AUROC of 79.4–82.8, and committing only unanimously supported states yields 81.0–100% success on 16–40% of the requests. These results establish world-state equivalence as an effective and inexpensive verification signal for stateful tool-using agents.

candidates.title: Certified Improvements to Best-Known Thomson-Problem Configurations with a Search Pipeline Built with Large Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: The Thomson problem asks for N unit charges on a sphere with minimum Coulomb energy; for large N the best configurations known are curated in the Cambridge Cluster Database, whose largest-N entries were set in October 2026. We report configurations for N = 912, 1382 and 2502 with energies 0.0036186, 0.0109730 and 0.0614033 below the database values, certified by exact integer arithmetic. All three are numerically strict local minima modulo rotations and keep the defect inventory and scar compositions of the database configurations; the database value for N = 912 had been reached by two different methods. Our search runs unconstrained replica-exchange basin hopping from the database configurations, with a shared pool of minima, recombination of improved regions after relabelling by geometry, and gradient-only polishing; replica-exchange basin hopping alone found the N = 912 and 1382 configurations, the former in one of five runs. We built and ran it with large language model agents (Claude, through a chat interface and the Claude Code agent), and we report every search, including those that failed. Two findings matter for others who search the database. Polishing alone lowers two entries by more than the threshold at which our pipeline reports a candidate, which produced two spurious records until candidates were compared with the polished database energies (the polished baseline). A local-relaxation speed-up passed its exactness test yet found nothing in a controlled comparison in which every arm with full relaxation went below the database value within 15 minutes. We distil three practices for computational discovery with large language model agents: calibrate the search code and verify candidates with code separate from the search, compare candidates with the polished baseline, and test design changes in controlled comparisons with pass criteria fixed in advance.

candidates.title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots
candidates.abstract: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use. We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none. On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $π_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself. On LIBERO-Pro, $π_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%. Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks. These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.

candidates.title: STAR-RAG: Structure-Aware Graph Retrieval for Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Knowledge Graphs
candidates.abstract: Knowledge graph retrieval-augmented generation (KG-RAG) provides structured evidence to support large language models (LLMs) in complex question answering. However, multi-hop graph expansion introduces weakly relevant relations, making it challenging to identify answer candidates supported by both question semantics and graph connectivity. Although existing graph retrievers exploit relational and structural information, effectively coordinating semantic message propagation, multi-order topological information, and candidate-level scoring remains challenging. To address these issues, we propose STAR-RAG, a structure-aware graph retrieval framework for multi-hop question answering. Specifically, Semantic noise routing (SNR) employs question-conditioned gates to regulate semantic messages before aggregation. Decoupled topological propagation (DTP) explicitly extracts directed degree and multi-order connectivity features and propagates structural information through a separate stream. Semantic-structural adaptive fusion (SSAF) then adaptively combines semantic and structural scores to rank answer candidates. The ranked candidates are connected to topic entities through evidence paths, which are provided to an LLM for answer generation. Experiments on WebQSP and CWQ show that STAR-RAG achieves retrieval Hit@1/F1 scores of 78.0/73.4 and 55.4/52.4, respectively. With Llama2-7B, generation Hit/F1 reaches 85.8/71.9 on WebQSP and 70.5/62.3 on CWQ. Ablation studies and diagnostic analyses further demonstrate the contributions of semantic routing, multi-order structural modeling, and adaptive fusion to retrieval performance.

candidates.title: Token Compression Technology for Large Language Model
candidates.abstract: The super long context window enables the large language model to realize the capabilities of long document question answering, multiple rounds of dialogue and retrieval enhancement generation, but the long token sequence will bring engineering bottlenecks such as high reasoning power, large memory occupation, and high interface call cost. The existing token compression technology can be divided into four types of mainstream solutions. Different methods are difficult to achieve balanced optimization between compression ratio, semantic fidelity, computational overhead and deployment cost, and to adapt to diversified business scenarios. This paper first combs the principles and takes textrank extraction algorithm with stop word filtering as the comparison baseline, and constructs two sets of differentiated compression frameworks for edge lightweight deployment and cloud high-precision reasoning. In this paper, a quantitative evaluation system including compression efficiency, semantic integrity and downstream task effect is established. The performance contribution of each module is quantified through ablation experiments. According to the experimental results, the scene selection strategy is given. The shortcomings of the existing schemes are analyzed and the future research directions are prospected, which provides theoretical and engineering support for the lightweight optimization of long context large model reasoning.

candidates.title: Decision Layers Matter More than Model Choice for Language-Model Agents: A Paired Evaluation in a Long-Horizon Business Simulation
candidates.abstract: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly entrusted with business decisions, yet their performance over long horizons is erratic. We examined whether coupling an agent with an external decision layer improves company management more than selecting a stronger model. On YC-Bench, a public benchmark in which an agent runs a start-up for one simulated year and is scored on final cash, eight LLMs were evaluated alone and with WhAI, a decision platform that estimates unobserved quantities from the history of the run and ranks candidate plans by Monte Carlo simulation of cash. In a paired test on four simulated worlds without published runs, all five tested models performed better with WhAI than alone in 48 of 48 pairs, with a mean gain of 1.72 million USD (95% CI 1.52–1.92; sign test p = 3.6 × 10−15). In additional analyses robust to clustering, the decision layer explained 72% of the variance in final cash, against 5% for the choice of model. On the published configuration, seven mid-size models with WhAI exceeded the best published model operating alone (3.45–3.82 versus 2.87 million USD) at up to one twentieth of its inference cost. In structured decision processes, the architecture surrounding a language model can matter more than the model itself.

candidates.title: Verifying Reasoning Chains Generated by Large Language Models: A Survey
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are extensively used for many Natural Language Processing tasks such as question answering, natural language inference, document summarization, etc. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting compels LLMs to generate step-by-step reasoning chains. While some of the reasoning chains may follow a correct thought process, they can also suffer from hallucinations, leading to errors in answer generation. Recently, many articles have targeted the problem of verifying these reasoning chains from various aspects. Despite this recent attention, to the best of our knowledge, no comprehensive survey currently summarizes these studies on reasoning chain verification. This work addresses that gap by presenting a detailed overview of the methods for verifying reasoning chains and categorizing them according to their methodology. This paper introduces a novel taxonomy of existing reasoning chain verification methods and mainly divides them into approaches that assess entire chains versus those that examine individual steps. This paper also reviews benchmarks for evaluating reasoning chains and verification methods and further discusses the challenges and future directions associated with these methods. By compiling and analyzing these approaches, our survey aims to advance the understanding and development of robust reasoning techniques in LLMs.

candidates.title: Large language models as oncology world models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can synthesize cancer patient cases, but their internal representation of oncology, or world model, has not been explored systematically. By only specifying tumor type, we show that LLMs tend to generate similar patients per cancer, with on average 81.0% to 93.2% of a cancer's patients sharing the most frequent value of each baseline feature. By systematically varying patient features in 12 clinical scenarios, we show that they follow biomarker and treatment logic in 29 of 36 model-scenario assessments, against 1 of 12 when previous treatment or frailty matters. Continuing real patient trajectories, an LLM predicted 89.9% 12-month survival, and 79.2% with similar patients as examples, against 72.2% observed. To represent these trajectories, we developed the Clinical State Space, a dynamic representation framework that we also applied to real patients. Despite the limits we show, improved world models may support digital twins, which our framework can evaluate.

candidates.title: Do Large Language Models Understand Financial Fraud?
candidates.abstract: Banks and compliance teams are exploring large language models (LLMs) as fraud analysts. Money laundering, however, is a structural crime. A single laundering transaction looks ordinary, and the evidence lies in how funds move across accounts. An LLM can only support anti-money-laundering (AML) work if it uses this structure rather than surface features. We test whether current LLMs do. We evaluate Claude, GPT-4.1, Phi-4, and Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite on 6,302 transactions from the IBM AML dataset. The benchmark keeps all 370 labeled laundering instances whole across eight typologies. We vary the context from a single transaction, to transaction history, to history with typology definitions and chain-of-thought reasoning. Only two of the four models beat chance, and only with the richest context. Their recall follows how often an account repeats within a laundering instance, not the shape of the instance. They detect hub-based typologies such as fan-in far better than bipartite or cycle typologies. The four models also rarely agree on which transactions are suspicious. These results suggest that current LLMs use repeated account activity as a proxy for fraud, and that they are not yet ready to serve as standalone AML detectors.

candidates.title: Comparison of Multimodal Large Language Models for Phytoplankton Identification from Microscopy Images
candidates.abstract: Phytoplankton composition and biomass are widely used indicators of eutrophication and aquatic ecosystem condition. Under the EU Water Framework Directive, phytoplankton is a biological quality element in ecological status assessment, which requires reliable taxonomic identification. This study evaluated the capabilities and limitations of general-purpose multimodal AI for phytoplankton identification from microscopy images using a two-stage design. In Stage 1, six off-the-shelf multimodal models—ChatGPT 5.1, ChatGPT 5.4, Gemini 3 Thinking, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Perplexity Pro and Grok 4.1—were compared using 30 expert-verified microscopy image cases. Gemini 3 Thinking showed the strongest overall performance across several measures, although no stable model hierarchy was established across all metrics. In Stage 2, GPT-5.6 Sol was evaluated using an expanded dataset of 157 microscopy images in three independent runs. Accuracy ranged from 70.1 to 81.5% at the higher-group level and from 40.1 to 57.3% at the genus level, but decreased to 14.3–31.8% at the species level. Performance differed significantly among runs and phytoplankton groups, with recurrent taxon-specific misclassification patterns. Across both stages, performance declined markedly with increasing taxonomic resolution. General-purpose multimodal AI may therefore support preliminary phytoplankton image screening and broad-group assignment, but current systems remain insufficiently reliable for autonomous genus- or species-level identification. Expert verification remains essential for ecological monitoring and water quality assessment.

candidates.title: Challenges of Single-Reference Benchmarks for Clinical Reasoning in Large Language Model–Based Decision Support
candidates.abstract: Unlabelled: This viewpoint addresses developers and evaluators of large language model (LLM)-based clinical decision support systems. Although recent benchmarks increasingly evaluate multiple clinical reasoning domains, many still rely substantially on reference decision agreement-whether model outputs conform to predefined decisions. Our aim is to clarify when such agreement remains useful, when it becomes insufficient for complex or preference-sensitive decisions, and how it can be complemented by reasoning-centered assessment. Clinical decision-making often depends on structured reasoning under uncertainty, integrating probabilistic evidence, contextual constraints, and patient values. Using oncology as an illustrative domain, we argue that some decision variability is a structural feature of clinical reasoning rather than noise or error. Used alone in such settings, single-reference benchmarks may conflate reasonable divergence with incorrectness and reward answer imitation over transparent reasoning. We conclude that reference decision agreement should be retained for tasks with stable ground truth but supplemented by evidence grounding, reasoning quality, patient-centeredness, and safety checks for open-ended clinical decision support. This multidimensional approach is intended to support safer and more clinically meaningful evaluation.

candidates.title: Adaptive Retrieval and Evidence Calibration for Reliable Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can expose a response to incorrect evidence when a retrieved source is plausible but mismatched. This paper presents ACRE, a compact pipeline that couples query-dependent reranking depth, source-evidence confidence estimation, and a selective output decision. A BM25 candidate list is augmented with lexical similarity signals; logistic confidence models select one, three, or five candidates and determine whether a verbatim, source-attributed answer should be issued. We evaluate on 300 authentic news reports and 50 out-of-index reports from the Lee text corpora, using 1,400 reproducibly derived source-identification queries. On the 280-query held-out split, adaptive retrieval matches the BM25 top-1 source accuracy of 77.86% while requiring only 1.73 candidates per query in the assigned reranking depth, versus five for the fixed-depth alternative. With the development-selected abstention threshold, the system responds to 80.36% of test queries at 91.11% accepted-source accuracy; its expected calibration error is 0.039. The results demonstrate an economical approach to coupling retrieval efficiency with calibrated source attribution in an explicitly extractive RAG setting.

candidates.title: Vision-Language-Action Models: A Life-Cycle Survey of Design, Training and Deployment
candidates.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt web-pretrained vision-language models to output robot actions, so that web knowledge carries over to physical control. In under 4 years the field has moved from RT-2, the first VLA, to open models that fine-tune on a single consumer GPU and to proprietary generalists that clean unseen homes. This survey reviews 88 works from December 2022 to October 2026, mainly on manipulation and navigation, plus humanoid control, world-action models and evaluation. We follow a VLA through its life cycle, from model design to training and deployment, along seven axes. Model design covers (a) inputs and memory, what the model observes; (b) architecture, how its pipeline is built; (c) action output, how it produces motor commands; and (d) intermediate predictions, what else it predicts, from reasoning steps to future observations. Training covers (e) pretraining data, the mix of robot, web, human and simulated data, and (f) post-training, adaptation to the target robot. Deployment covers (g) real-time execution, keeping pace with the robot. We analyse 22 models on these axes and report their training data, model size, inference speed and hardware. Three trends emerge: (i) training data has broadened, from about 10,000 hours of teleoperated robot data ($π_0$) to 23,000 community-collected episodes (SmolVLA) and 20,000 hours of egocentric human video (GR00T N1.7); (ii) model sizes have split: most recent models have 3-7 billion parameters, while a new group under one billion runs on consumer GPUs; and (iii) generalist VLAs are emerging that handle both manipulation and navigation, such as UniVLA and Qwen-VLA. We also compare VLAs with world-action models, which predict future observations as well as actions. We review evidence that some VLAs with near-perfect benchmark scores fail when objects or the camera move slightly, and open up further research questions.

candidates.title: Query-Aware Context Compression for Efficient Long-Context Language Model Inference
candidates.abstract: Query-aware context compression can reduce the amount of source text forwarded to a language model, but keyword ranking may discard evidence connected through intermediate entities. We present QAB-R, a training-free sentence selector combining BM25, query-identifier-constrained anchor selection, canonicalized entity matching, and at most two bridge-linked candidates under a fixed sentence budget. We first evaluate a single-bridge baseline on 300 synthetic single- and two-hop queries. We then execute 300 additional held-out stress cases covering paraphrases, competing entity notes, identifier formatting variation, and combined changes; a separate 60-case test extends source contexts to 58,368 whitespace-delimited words. At a 10% sentence budget, QAB-R preserved complete two-hop support in all 60 cases of each stress condition, whereas single-bridge retention fell to 0% under competing notes and format changes. For 1,024 fact pairs, the median QAB-R CPU preprocessing time was 66.3 ms, and the selected text contained 5,741 of 58,368 input words. The study reports evidence completeness, retained input length, and CPU preprocessing cost; downstream reader accuracy and GPU inference speed are distinct system-level outcomes.

candidates.title: Ontology-Guided, Verifiable In-Silico Experiments on Lumped-Parameter Cardiovascular Models: Semantic Connection Checking, SHACL Validation and a Receipt-Verified Language-Model Agent
candidates.abstract: Composing physiological models from independent components fails at the joints: same-unit variables can carry different meanings, metadata can be correct while the attached numbers are wrong, and a language model that writes the report can state results never computed. We present an open framework treating each separately. The core is a deterministic six-compartment closed-loop cardiovascular model integrated as a hybrid system of valve regimes with runtime conservation, positivity, valve and settling audits. A semantic layer annotates 34 variables with label-checked Ontology of Physics for Biology properties and Uberon/FMA anatomy, exports named-graph RDF and provides a fail-closed connection validator requiring agreement of property, anatomy, bearer, reference, temporal context and flow orientation before a value is transferred. In a 12-fixture fault-injection benchmark it rejects eight of nine unsafe connections an unguarded baseline accepts; its retained blind spot, correct left-ventricular metadata on right-ventricular data, passes with errors up to 129.8 mmHg. An evidence-first review of the Smith et al. (2004) CellML model produced a variable dictionary, anatomical node specification, SHACL shapes and PROV-O records; on the model’s published SemSim annotation they report 22 violations, 7 warnings and 46 informational results. A tool-calling language-model agent plans baseline-versus-intervention experiments under a three-layer scope guard; it chooses only runs and metric paths, and every sentence and number in its report is written by code from tool receipts and re-verified. In a 27-case evaluation three providers passed every case; all 14 out-of-scope clinical requests were refused before any model call. Nothing is clinically validated; parameters are exploratory, claim boundaries stated. Code, evidence (redacted where required), shapes, provenance and traces are public.

candidates.title: Continuous-Space Diffusion and Flow Language Models: A Survey
candidates.abstract: Continuous-space diffusion and flow language models generate text by updating real-valued vectors (such as token embeddings, compressed codes, or sentence vectors) and decoding them into discrete words at readout. We organize this literature by three coupled choices: the continuous state being refined, the transition operator that updates it, and the text interface that converts states into tokens. Because language is discrete while the state space is continuous, adapting image diffusion to text encounters rounding ambiguity and embedding collapse under squared-error regression, uninformative noise schedules, distribution shift between clean-text codecs and learned priors, and mode averaging in few-step sampling. Across published comparisons with autoregressive and discrete-diffusion baselines, continuous models show no general advantage over same-scale autoregressive models on open-ended text; the closest prompt-continuation tie uses different training sequence lengths and separately tuned samplers. RePlaid matches or improves upon masked diffusion in likelihood bounds past compute-optimal budgets, and large-scale blockwise adaptation brings continuous models close to masked baselines on mathematical reasoning and code; however, continuous models still trail autoregressive baselines in held-out likelihood bounds, and scaling fits indicate that matching exact autoregressive negative log-likelihood requires substantially more training compute. Their clearest gains over autoregressive decoding appear in gradient-guided control, plan-level diversity, and task-specific reasoning after targeted fine-tuning. Under few-step budgets, trajectory-consistent distillation and stochastic bridges prevent entropy collapse, yet no standalone continuous generator has shown an end-to-end latency win over optimized autoregressive decoding at matched quality; the reported matched-quality latency gains rely on autoregressive verification of continuous drafts. We close with open problems in likelihood scaling, readout fidelity, few-step serving, representation reuse, and post-training.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): Enhancing LLMs with External Knowledge
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) generate fluent answers, but they depend mainly on their training data. As a result they can give wrong or outdated responses, and they may lack the specific information a question needs. Retraining a model again and again to fix this takes a great deal of time. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses the problem by retrieving relevant information from external knowledge sources, such as documents, databases and the web, before a response is generated. This paper presents a literature survey and problem understanding for RAG. It explains the retrieve–augment–generate workflow, states the problem and six objectives, and relates RAG to current technology trends: real-time information, enterprise AI, agentic AI, cost-effective scalability and reduced hallucination. Eight studies from 2020 to 2026 are compared on methodology, key findings and limitations. The analysis reveals that the quality of information retrieval, as well as the effectiveness, accuracy and assessment, still remain unstudied topics. Four research gaps are identified: high computational resources, irrelevant or incomplete retrieval, limited effectiveness in specialised domains, and the need for better evaluation of factuality, relevance and reliability.

candidates.title: Large language model agents with simulation-trained surrogates retrieve multi-objective reservoir development plans from hierarchical knowledge graphs
candidates.abstract: Optimizing oilfield development is a high-dimensional, multi-objective decision problem: candidate plans must balance hydrocarbon recovery against economic return while satisfying operational constraints. Retrieval methods that rank evidence by textual or structural similarity cannot express such trade-offs or reject infeasible plans, whereas full-physics simulation is too costly to run inside an interactive search. We present PHARAOH, a framework in which a large language model agent retrieves development plans over a multi-resolution knowledge graph, guided by a simulation-trained surrogate model that estimates objectives such as ultimate recovery and net present value. The agent combines global anchoring with type-filtered hierarchical refinement and aggregates parallel search trajectories into a set of diverse recommendations; its policy is then distilled into a compact student model. PHARAOH screens and ranks candidates within a pre-built decision space rather than solving a continuous optimization problem. On PetroGraph, a benchmark built from three public reservoir simulation models, PHARAOH attains the best average performance among the compared baselines, improving Hit@1 by 8.8 and Recall@20 by 7.1 over a surrogate-guided non-agentic search. Full-physics re-simulation shows that 14 of 15 top-ranked plans satisfy the operational constraints, although near-boundary plans remain sensitive to surrogate error. The distilled 7B student retains about 85% of the teacher’s Hit@1 at a fraction of the inference cost. These findings are limited to three simulation benchmarks; field-scale validation remains future work.

candidates.title: Automating postmarketing pharmacovigilance with large language model agents
candidates.abstract: Postmarketing pharmacovigilance relies on spontaneous adverse event reporting and labor-intensive observational studies, which suffer from underreporting and delayed risk detection. Large language model (LLM) agents could automate real-world evidence generation, but generalist agents make ad hoc analytical decisions that compromise epidemiological validity and reproducibility. Here we present MedCheckpoint, a multi-agent LLM system for automated postmarketing pharmacovigilance. MedCheckpoint grounds each analytical stage in a curated, source-traceable medical knowledge base, locks core study-design parameters before execution, performs patient-level analyses with human-written deterministic statistical tools, and enforces checkpoint rules that abort infeasible analyses, with optional human-in-the-loop review. We evaluated MedCheckpoint using a 54-question benchmark on a dual-purpose simulated electronic health record (EHR) testbed of 2.7 million individuals, designed with reliable clinical signals to evaluate routine analytical accuracy alongside spurious signals to stress-test system rigor. Across the benchmark, MedCheckpoint outperformed two coding-agent baselines in report quality across five dimensions rated by three independent LLM judges (overall means 4.81-4.88 versus 4.25-4.55 and 4.02-4.29) and yielded higher run-to-run consistency (mean within-question standard deviation 0.116-0.186 versus up to 0.440). Crucially, while baselines failed on up to 2 of 21 runs when handling infeasible comparisons or unmeasurable outcomes, MedCheckpoint produced no misleading failures across all seven stress-test trap questions with known data limitations. MedCheckpoint enables reliable, auditable, and scalable pharmacovigilance analysis.

candidates.title: Human or Synthetic? What a Fixed Budget Buys for Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Post-training of large language models typically combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with preference-based fine-tuning such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Human-annotated and synthetically generated preference data differ substantially in per-sample cost, but prior work typically holds sample count fixed when comparing the two. In this work, we explicitly study the interplay between cost and performance by comparing the effect of post-training with human and synthetic preference data under a fixed, dollar-matched annotation budget. We train and evaluate multiple base model families across helpfulness and summarization tasks. We find that synthetic data is far more cost-efficient at low-to-moderate budgets, achieving high win rates with as little as \$200--\$400. On helpfulness, human data closes the gap only at budgets roughly two orders of magnitude larger; on summarization, it does not close the gap at any tested budget. We also find that human-annotated data varies in reliability: one widely used human preference source substantially underperforms another, and the gap persists even after standard remedies such as domain restriction and deduplication.

candidates.title: Multimodal retrieval-augmented generation for domain knowledge enhancement in large language models
candidates.abstract: Large language models are susceptible to problems such as lagging parameter knowledge updates, insufficient alignment of textual and graphical evidence, and incomplete factual basis for answers in domain-specific question answering. To address these issues, a domain-consistent multimodal retrieval enhancement generation framework, DC-MRAG, is proposed. This framework comprises four modules: domain anchor index, hierarchical cross-modal retrieval, evidence consistency fusion, and uncertainty-aware generation. It achieves unified representation of textual and graphical evidence through domain concept constraints, utilizes multi-factor scoring for candidate recall and re-ranking, compresses context based on evidence support, and controls generation risk through confidence calibration and selective secondary retrieval. Under a unified example experimental setting, the proposed method achieves an exact match rate of 84.9%, a recall@5 rate of 91.4%, an answer fidelity of 94.2%, and a phantom rate reduction to 4.6%. Compared to RAMQA, the exact match rate is improved by 4.2 percentage points, the phantom rate is relatively reduced by 41.03%, context tokens are reduced by 26.99%, P95 response latency is reduced by 23.43%, and throughput is increased by 28.85%. The results show that the collaborative design of domain indexing, cross-modal retrieval, evidence fusion, and generative calibration can improve the accuracy, evidence reliability, and online service efficiency of knowledge-based question answering.

candidates.title: InceptionRAG: Stealthy Poisoning Attack Against Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems enhance large language models (LLMs) with external knowledge but have been demonstrated vulnerable to corpus poisoning. Existing poisoning attacks against RAG largely focus on single-point explicit injection, where the malicious payload is fully encapsulated within a single document. Consequently, recent mitigation mechanisms have evolved to identify and diminish these threats effectively. In this paper, we first verify that existing mitigation mechanisms are insufficient for a new class of threats: indirect logic induction. Motivated by this observation, we introduce InceptionRAG, a stealthy attack mechanism that subverts the standard attack paradigm. Instead of injecting explicit malicious payloads, InceptionRAG fragments it into a chain of dormant passages. These passages appear harmless and can bypass existing mitigation mechanisms when examined separately. However, when retrieved together, they trigger LLMs to self-deduce target misinformation via multi-hop reasoning. To further improve the applicability of InceptionRAG in black-box settings, we propose zeroth-order suffix optimization (ZOSO) to automate the generation of authoritative suffixes. Extensive evaluations across three datasets and three LLMs demonstrate that InceptionRAG achieves an attack success rate exceeding 80% even under rigorous adversarial constraints. In particular, InceptionRAG shows superior evasion capabilities, effectively bypassing established defenses that mitigate traditional single-document injections. Our findings expose a concerning paradox: The stronger reasoning capabilities of LLMs increase their vulnerability to reasoning-based poisoning attacks. To mitigate the potential misuse of InceptionRAG, we propose a document isolation-based defense HODOR, which effectively mitigates the attack by decoupling the adversarial logical dependencies.

candidates.title: Securing Software in the Age of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer new capabilities for software security by interpreting source code and natural-language specifications, and generating plausible code. However, their probabilistic behavior, hallucinations, limited security knowledge, and inconsistent outputs make their direct use non-trivial. This dissertation investigates how LLMs can identify code requiring protection, discover and repair vulnerabilities in existing software, and improve the security of generated software code while accounting for reliability and deployment costs. The completed research provides results across three settings. LLM-CAL identifies cryptographic code for fine-grained TEE boundary establishment, reducing the Trusted Computing Base by 81.20%. RESTing-LLAMA uses semantic OpenAPI documentation to discover 11 vulnerabilities across real-world REST APIs with fewer requests and a lower false-positive rate than existing fuzzers. RAVEN combines agentic retrieval, repository-level dependency analysis, and iterative refinement to achieve an 83.13% repair success rate across 160 real-world CVE instances. The ongoing research examines the trustworthiness of LLM-based code generation through knowledge-poisoning attacks against RACG systems and an agentic Graph RAG framework for retrieving CWE-structured security knowledge. Together, these studies examine how LLMs can be adapted for securing existing and generated software.

candidates.title: Enhancing capability boundaries of in-context learning in large language models for computer vision
candidates.abstract: Visual context learning enables large language models to perform visual question answering and cross-scene reasoning based on a limited number of image and text examples. However, its performance is limited by factors such as example redundancy, visual token overhead, insufficient cross-modal alignment, and prediction confidence bias. To address these issues, this paper proposes a boundary-enhanced visual context learning framework, BEV-ICL. It improves the task relevance and structural diversity of examples through boundary-aware example selection and rearrangement, preserves key objects and spatial relationships using structure-aware visual token compression, achieves dynamic alignment of visual evidence with question semantics through relational conditional gating, and enhances output reliability through uncertainty-aware reasoning and probability calibration. In the constructed experimental scheme, the average accuracy of the proposed method reached 69.6%, an improvement of 4.4 percentage points compared to the comparison method. The long context accuracy increased from 57.3% to 68.9%; the number of context tokens decreased from 5120 to 3200, a reduction of 37.50%; the average inference latency decreased from 428.6 ms to 286.4 ms , a reduction of 33.18%; P95 latency decreased by 34.29%; system throughput increased from 22.4 req/s to 33.8 req/s, an increase of 50.89%; and the expected calibration error decreased from 6.8% to 4.1%. These results demonstrate that jointly optimizing example configuration, visual structure compression, cross-modal relationships, and prediction calibration can expand the applicability of visual context learning in terms of task performance, context capacity, and inference efficiency.

candidates.title: DRAMA: Dissecting Attention Redundancy for Accelerating Multimodal Diffusion Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate text through iterative masked denoising with bidirectional attention, offering a compelling alternative to autoregressive vision-language modeling. However, each denoising step requires a full forward pass over long multimodal sequences in which visual tokens dominate the sequence length, and a fixed step budget further compounds this quadratic per-step cost. Existing inference acceleration approaches for multimodal dLLMs characterize attention redundancy implicitly, motivating designs from isolated attention visualizations rather than from measurement. We close this gap with DRAMA, a training-free acceleration framework grounded in a systematic dissection of attention redundancy in multimodal dLLMs. By probing attention tensors along spatial and temporal axes, we reveal two persistent redundancy structures: (i) attention mass consistently concentrates on a sparse subset of visual tokens, and (ii) attention distributions rapidly stabilize across denoising steps after an initial formation phase. These findings motivate two complementary mechanisms: Spatial-Redundancy-Aware Visual Token Pruning (SVTP) and Sufficiency-Guided Adaptive Stopping (SGAS). Together, DRAMA achieves an average 18.67 times inference speedup across six vision-language benchmarks without training, architectural modification, or attention caching, while maintaining competitive accuracy. Our results establish a strong, measurement-grounded acceleration baseline for multimodal dLLM inference.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Chatbot for Academic Information Services Using GROQ API
candidates.abstract: Academic information services in universities are still largely carried out manually by administrative staff with limited working hours, making it difficult for students to receive quick responses, especially outside office hours. This study aims to design and implement an academic chatbot using the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approach through the Groq API and a Streamlit interface. The system was developed following the Design Science Research (DSR) methodology, which includes problem identification, defining solution objectives, dataset collection, artifact design and development, system demonstration, testing and evaluation, as well as communication of research results. Black-box testing on 20 questions yielded 18 valid answers, while semantic quality evaluation using BERTScore produced a precision of 0.7054, recall of 0.7176, and F1-score of 0.7095. The average system response time was 1.45 seconds, with a median of 0.85 seconds, indicates that the majority of responses were provided in less than one second, despite a single outlier of 12.13 seconds. These results finding suggest that the integration of RAG with the Groq API holds potential for enhancing digital academic information services in higher education. Nevertheless, its operational benefits in real-world scenarios warrant further evaluation through empirical user testing.

candidates.title: Programming Quantum Circuit Parameters with Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated the ability to generate parameters for variational quantum circuits without conventional optimization. However, the conditions under which this approach is effective remain unclear. Here, we investigate a frozen, general-purpose LLM that generates complete circuit parameter vectors from symbolic circuit and Hamiltonian descriptions, with optional iterative energy feedback. We evaluate the approach on general random Hamiltonians, structured parent Hamiltonians, and molecular systems. For general Hamiltonians, LLM-generated parameters exhibit larger energy errors than conventional Adam optimization, while additional feedback generally provides limited improvement. In contrast, for structured Hamiltonians, the LLM can generate promising low-energy parameter configurations, suggesting that identifiable physical and mathematical structure facilitates parameter inference. We also show that direct LLM predictions of minimum energies can violate the Hamiltonian spectral lower bound, whereas generated circuit parameters allow independent evaluation of physically realizable energy expectation values. Finally, we investigate blind circuit interpretation and find that the LLM can predict measurement outcomes even when it fails to identify the underlying quantum algorithm. These findings highlight the role of problem structure, the limitations of iterative LLM optimization, and the importance of independently verifiable predictions in quantum parameter programming.

candidates.title: MMAligner: Safeguarding Multimodal Large Language Models through Representation Calibration
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a wide range of generative tasks. However, introducing non-text modalities poses significant challenges for safety alignment. MLLMs often refuse unsafe text-only prompts while producing harmful responses to semantically equivalent multimodal inputs. Existing mitigation strategies, including external guardrails and safety-oriented fine-tuning, largely overlook the mechanisms driving this safety disparity. External guardrails merely circumvent the model's intrinsic defects, while safety-oriented fine-tuning treats alignment as a black-box optimization problem, failing to diagnose and repair this flaw specifically. As a result, these methods either incur substantial inference latency with limited protection or significantly compromise model utility and rely heavily on large-scale multimodal datasets. Consequently, achieving effective and utility-preserving safety alignment for MLLMs remains an unresolved challenge. In this paper, we conduct a geometric analysis of MLLM representations to investigate the causes of multimodal safety degradation. We reveal that the safety mechanisms learned in the text-only modality actually persist in the multimodal setting. The safety subspace with refusal boundary remains valid across different modalities, where representations falling inside this boundary consistently elicit safe refusal responses. However, we observe a critical shift in representation where most unsafe multimodal inputs fall outside the boundary and bypass this intrinsic mechanism. This finding identifies the root cause of safety failure in the multimodal setting as a representation shift rather than a lack of safety capability. Motivated by this observation, we propose MMAligner, an MLLM safeguarding method based on representation calibration. Unlike existing methods, MMAligner addresses this representation shift by optimizing the model to map unsafe multimodal representations inside the pre-existing refusal boundary. Specifically, it adopts a hard lower bound to ensure refusal and a soft upper bound to prevent excessive modification, while preserving the representation of benign inputs. Extensive experiments on multiple open-source MLLMs demonstrate that MMAligner increases the average refusal rate of multimodal unsafe inputs to 99% while incurring less than 2% utility degradation using minimal data, significantly outperforming existing baselines in the safety-utility trade-off.

candidates.title: Large language models for mental health
candidates.abstract: Digital technologies have long been explored as a complement to standard procedure in mental health research and practice, ranging from the management of electronic health records to app-based interventions. The recent emergence of large language models (LLMs), both proprietary and open-source ones, represents a major new opportunity on that front. Yet there is still a divide between the community developing LLMs and the one which may benefit from them, thus hindering the beneficial translation of the technology into clinical use. This divide largely stems from the lack of a common language and understanding regarding the technology’s inner workings, capabilities, and risks. Our tutorial-style review attempts to bridge this gap by providing intuitive explanations behind the basic concepts related to contemporary LLMs.

candidates.title: Hyperbolic Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Abstract. Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success and demonstrated superior performance across various tasks, including natural language processing (NLP), weather forecasting, biological protein folding, text generation, and solving mathematical problems. However, many real-world data exhibit highly non-Euclidean latent hierarchical anatomy, such as protein networks, transportation networks, financial networks, brain networks, and linguistic structures or syntactic trees in natural languages. Effectively learning intrinsic semantic entailment and hierarchical relationships from these raw, unstructured input data using LLMs remains an underexplored area. Due to its effectiveness in modeling tree-like hierarchical structures, hyperbolic geometry—a non-Euclidean space—has rapidly gained popularity as an expressive latent representation space for complex data modeling across domains such as graphs, images, languages, and multimodal data. Here, we provide a comprehensive and contextual exposition of recent advancements in LLMs that leverage hyperbolic geometry as a representation space to enhance semantic representation learning and multiscale reasoning. Specifically, the paper presents a taxonomy of the principal techniques of hyperbolic LLMs (HypLLMs) in terms of four main categories: (1) hyperbolic LLMs through exp/log maps; (2) hyperbolic fine-tuned models; (3) fully hyperbolic LLMs; and (4) hyperbolic state-space models. We also explore crucial potential applications and outline future research directions. A repository of key papers, models, datasets, and code implementations is available at https://github.com/sarangp2402/Hyperbolic-LLM-Models .

candidates.title: Evolutionary Trajectories in Large Language Models: From Transformers to Reasoning-Augmented Systems
candidates.abstract: The accelerated evolution of the Large Language Models (LLM) has taken natural linguistic processing to the next phase of transformer-based frameworks to more sophisticated tools, including GPT-3 and GPT-4. Regardless of the enhancement in fluency and usefulness that scaling laws and alignment techniques introduced, the issue of hallucination still remains a scourge of the flesh with models producing realistically false or misleading results. As a method of handling this weakness, there has to exist structured reasoning and checking in the LLM pipelines. The given paper explains the development of the LLMs into the reasoning-enhanced systems and evaluates the following strategies used in TruthfulQA: Baseline, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), ReAct, and Self-Consistency. The findings reveal that reasoning augmentation can potentially decrease hallucinations by up to 1520 and accuracy by 3040 percent compared to models that only use basic reasoning methods, which could be increased at the expense of increased computational latency. Sensitivity studies too demonstrate how incorporated tools and sampling would come in handy in providing factual underpinning. This paper provides the identification of tradeoffs between accuracy, efficiency, and reliability and the significance of hybrid verification pipelines in future LLMs.

candidates.title: CapLite: Prompt-Injection Defense for Small Language Model Agents without Model-Written Security Artifacts
candidates.abstract: Enforcement defenses against prompt injection, such as CaMeL, Progent, IPIGuard and DRIFT, ask the agent's own model to write a security artifact (a program, a privilege policy, a dependency graph or a constraint list) that code then enforces. We ask whether small language model (SLM) agents can be trusted to write these artifacts. Across 15 open-weight models, 13 of them between 1.7B and 12B parameters, they cannot: the policies, graphs and constraints that the agent's model writes admit attacks on 14 (Progent), 13 (IPIGuard) and 11 (DRIFT) of the models, and CaMeL's programs fail to run in up to 68% of episodes. We present CapLite, which derives its policy from the tool schemas, commits the write calls before any tool result is read, and admits a write only if every argument that decides whom or what it affects is stated in the user's request. This guarantees write integrity: injected text cannot add a write, and no write reaches a recipient, amount, object or destination that the user did not state. No attack succeeds in 13,935 attacked AgentDojo episodes. CapLite reaches utility under attack comparable to CaMeL's (29.0% vs. 27.2%) with fewer tokens than every other enforcement defense and than the undefended agent: 17.1k per episode, 18% of CaMeL's, and the highest utility per token of all enforcement defenses.

candidates.title: Agentic-Teacher: An Agentic Data Engine for Failure-Driven VLA Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Improving a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model requires demonstrations that address its weaknesses and provide effective supervision for learning. Coding agents can autonomously generate demonstrations through environment interaction, yet successful execution alone does not ensure effective supervision for VLA learning. We introduce Agentic-Teacher, an autonomous data engine for failure-driven VLA post-training. Given a VLA checkpoint, a task specification, and configured environment tools, the engine analyzes failed rollouts, selects intervention states, and iteratively develops closed-loop code policies through execution feedback. Validated policies become reusable demonstration generators that collect successful continuations from states where the VLA struggles. To make these demonstrations suitable for learning, Agentic-Teacher introduces temporally correlated action noise to broaden state-action coverage, removes idle frames while preserving gripper transitions, and filters trajectories using the frozen base model's flow-matching loss. The resulting demonstrations are combined with successful VLA rollouts for post-training, yielding an updated policy that operates without coding-agent assistance. Agentic-Teacher thus connects the weaknesses of a target VLA to both the generation and curation of its training data. In simulation, it improves $π_0$ success rates from 79.4% to 87.8% on LIBERO-10, from 80.4% to 90.6% on MetaWorld-10, and from 0% to 30.0% across three RoboCasa tasks.

candidates.title: Active Learning of Approximate LLM Ranking for Energy-Efficient Retrieval of Long Queries
candidates.abstract: Search engines and Large Language Models (LLMs) offer complementary strengths for document retrieval: lexical retrievers which rely on keyword matching are fast and energy-efficient, whereas LLMs capture semantic meaning and excel at interpreting long, context-rich queries. However, this comes at a cost that is computationally and energetically prohibitive. We propose the LLM Active Approximation Model (LAAM), a hybrid retrieval framework that introduces a lightweight learned predictor which serves as an intermediary between semantic retrieval and LLM retrieval. LAAM is refined through an active learning loop where an LLM labels a small number of documents. By concentrating LLM evaluations on the most informative documents, the framework substantially reduces inference cost while preserving retrieval effectiveness. We evaluate the proposed framework on TREC Robust 2004 using Lucene with BM25 retrieval and DeepSeek v3 as the LLM, under three levels of query verbosity. For verbose queries, LAAM achieves 87% of average P@10 achieved by DeepSeek's reranking (0.459 vs. 0.526), while requiring only 3.3% of the per-query energy consumption. LAAM is statistically significantly better than BM25 and is indistinguishable from DeepSeek on average precision, though not on MAP (Friedman test, P<0.05 with post-hoc testing). Overall, our results demonstrate that selectively approximating LLM relevance judgments through active learning enables retrieval accuracy to be controlled directly through the evaluation (and consequently energy) budget. Rather than committing to either inexpensive (and less accurate) lexical retrieval or exhaustive (and expensive) LLM reranking, our framework exposes a continuous spectrum of operating points along the energy--accuracy curve, allowing practitioners to select how to trade retrieval quality with computational budget.

candidates.title: VisText-VLM2Plastic: A Bilingual Benchmark for Visual Grounding and Environmental Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Abstract Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly support open-ended visual reasoning, yet their behavior in low-resource languages and sustainability-oriented domains remains underexplored. We introduce a controlled English–Bangla plastic-waste VQA benchmark comprising 402 image records derived from 136 base images and 2,412 question–answer pairs across five waste categories and three task types: recognition, visual description, and environmental reasoning. We evaluate GPT-4.1 mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-4B zero-shot using task-specific answer-quality metrics, bilingual consistency, and image ablation. Gemini 2.5 Flash yields the highest recognition point estimate, with 93.5% accuracy and 91.3% macro-F1. Across models, English normalized performance exceeds Bangla by 3.78 points on average, with the largest observed gap for environmental reasoning. Removing the image reduces normalized performance by 66.29 points for recognition, 52.89 for description, and 11.42 for environmental reasoning. The smaller environmental-reasoning ablation gap indicates that, in this benchmark, many environmental questions remain partly answerable from linguistic and domain priors. These results show why answer quality alone is insufficient for multilingual multimodal evaluation and motivate reporting cross-lingual consistency and sensitivity to visual evidence alongside conventional metrics.

candidates.title: Cited but Unused: Parametric Provenance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation systems attach citations to attribute claims to their sources. These citations frequently misstate provenance, and standard verification cannot detect this. We measure provenance by counterfactual value substitution: a fact in the retrieved passages is replaced with a false variant and the model re-queried. We find that across five sizes of one model family and a second comparator family, 1.2% to 15.7% of citable claims derive from parametric memory rather than the retrieved context. At the most conservative substitution distance these figures are 4.6% and 8.5% on the two models we tested at it, with the rate rising with model size within a family. We further find that natural language inference verification, the standard approach, gives results indistinguishable from chance across models, even when restricted to the cited passage. We determine that the cause is structural: a model answering from memory selects a citation that agrees with its output. Comparing ten attribution methods on identical claims, the contrast between the model's distribution with and without context best separates provenance. Acting on that signal does not improve provenance honesty at these base rates. The resulting detector is hence still not accurate enough to act on: it measures what the model knew rather than what it used, and separating those remains the open problem.

candidates.title: Thinking Dangerously: How Reasoning Training Dilutes Safety in Language Models
candidates.abstract: Ask a reasoning model a harmful question and it refuses; ask it again after a long, entirely benign reasoning chain and it answers. Across six open-weight models, average refusal falls from 94.6% to 12.7% behind an 8,192-token benign prefix. We name this failure Safety Dilution and make it measurable: refusal decays smoothly with length, so each model has an L50, the prefix length at which refusal falls below one half, within a few thousand tokens, and the form-free Area Under the Bypass Curve (AUBC) makes the erosion comparable across models. In one matched-parameter, same-pretraining-base family, reasoning training doubles AUBC, though the effect also appears in models without it. Length-monotone safety is one of three properties a chain is assumed to have; the other two break as readily. Premise Corruption plants a false premise that the model's own inference propagates through the chain, largely evading prompt-injection defenses. Reasoning Chain Injection forges steps that match the model's own continuation distribution, blunting coherence checks wherever reasoning tokens are exposed. ChainGuard checks all three properties at runtime without retraining, cutting attack success by 56.3 percentage points on average; its truncation-only default recovers over half of that at 6% overhead. The gap does not close, but an adaptive adversary pays roughly two orders of magnitude more compute per success. Safety that holds for a sentence but dissolves over a chain is not safety: alignment has to hold over the whole computation, not just its opening tokens.
