candidates.title: Causal consistency for long chain-of-thought reasoning in large language models
candidates.abstract: Chain-of-Thought prompting has become a widely used strategy for improving the reasoning ability of large language models. More recently, Long Chain-of-Thought prompting has extended this strategy by allowing models to generate longer and more detailed reasoning trajectories. While this often benefits complex tasks, such as mathematical problem solving, logical inference, and commonsense reasoning, the quality of the generated reasoning is not determined by its length alone. Long reasoning chains may still include redundant steps, weak causal dependencies, inconsistent intermediate conclusions, or transitions that are not well supported by previous steps. These issues make it difficult to determine whether the reasoning process is faithful, interpretable, and reliable. In this paper, we propose a causal consistency framework for analyzing and improving Long Chain-of-Thought reasoning in large language models. We formulate extended reasoning trajectories under a Structural Causal Model and divide them into causally structured sub-chains. We then evaluate the causal contribution and counterfactual reliability of each reasoning segment using Interventional Value and Counterfactual Fidelity. To connect local verification with the final answer, we further introduce a global causal consistency metric that jointly considers structural propagation and answer-level stability. The proposed framework provides a way to move Long Chain-of-Thought reasoning beyond merely generating longer explanations toward producing reasoning chains that are causally grounded and verifiable. Experimental results on mathematical, logical, and commonsense reasoning benchmarks indicate that our method reduces redundant reasoning steps, strengthens causal coherence, and improves the robustness of long-form reasoning.

Recent work has begun to study conflicts among modalities, but a conflict does not necessarily indicate that a person is concealing an emotion. It may also result from mixed emotions, individual expressive styles, or contextual factors. This proposal aims to distinguish ordinary emotional inconsistency from emotion concealment and to infer the underlying emotion when supported by evidence. We plan to construct a multimodal benchmark with explicit annotations of expressed emotion, internal emotion, and concealment conditions, and to develop an MLLM-based framework that integrates fine-grained facial Action Units (AUs), cross-modal features, and temporal context.

candidates.title: HiRAG: A Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework via Intent Routing and Small-Model Refinement
candidates.abstract: While retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mitigates large language model (LLM) hallucinations, traditional flat vector retrieval in massive, heterogeneous databases suffers from high latency and noise interference. To address this, we propose HiRAG, a hierarchical RAG framework. Offline, HiRAG builds a “classification-summary” dual-layer index to structurally organize data. Online, a lightweight bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT)-based router identifies query intent to dynamically prune the search space. A cascaded pipeline then uses hybrid retrieval and Small-LLM reranking for coarse-to-fine de-noising. Experiments on the Microsoft Machine Reading Comprehension (MS MARCO) and Multi-Domain Enterprise Knowledge Base (MDE-KB) datasets demonstrate that HiRAG outperforms traditional baselines. Specifically on MDE-KB, HiRAG improves Recall@5 by 14.5 percentage points over Naive RAG and achieves a retrieval augmented generation assessment (RAGAS) Answer Relevance score of 0.92, while reducing average query latency by 28%. HiRAG provides a viable, efficient solution for large-scale knowledge bases.

candidates.title: GateTrim: Adaptive-Rank Quantization for Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: We introduce GateTrim, an adaptive-rank post-training quantization method for large language models that learns matrix-specific ranks through gate optimization and threshold-based rank selection. GateTrim standardizes the low-rank factors of a quantized low-rank--residual representation, learns a separate gate vector for each target weight matrix, and uses a shared threshold to automatically determine its retained rank. The resulting ranks can differ across matrices, and the compact quantized representations are subsequently reconstructed. We evaluate GateTrim under W4A8 on Qwen3-4B/8B/14B, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Across all five models, we observe a counterintuitive finding: increasing the threshold from $τ=0.3$ to $τ=0.7$ reduces the mean retained rank by 46.60%--67.89% while simultaneously lowering WikiText-2 perplexity by 0.59%--5.17%. Threshold 0.7 achieves the lowest mean retained rank and final perplexity among the three tested thresholds, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7, and reduces measured target-export size by 1.50%--4.25% relative to 0.3. GateTrim uses an $8\times512$-token fitting pool and a separate development pool of the same size. Its Qwen3-4B/8B/14B perplexities at $τ=0.7$ are numerically below TwinQuant's published W4A8 values, reported with a $128\times2048$-token calibration pool, in a cross-study comparison. On Qwen3-8B, the threshold-0.7 configuration already has the lowest perplexity before reconstruction under both tested initialization seeds; reconstruction improves it further without increasing retained rank or export size.

candidates.title: Authorization-Aware Multi-Agent Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Secure Enterprise Knowledge Access
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enables language models to answer enterprise questions using external documents; however semantic retrieval and multi-agent delegation create authorization risks when access checks occur only after search or answer generation. This study presents a literature-informed architecture for authorization-aware multi-agent RAG in which a policy decision point evaluates current user and resource attributes, whereas a policy enforcement point restricts the eligible candidate set before content reaches rerankers, agents, or a large language model. This design combines role-based and attribute-based access control, semantic embeddings, vector search, least-privilege delegation, provenance-aware auditing, and policy revalidation at protected access boundaries. A focused survey identifies risks including semantic overfetch, cross-domain synthesis leakage, stale permissions, and delegation escalation. The paper defines authorization-correctness conditions and proposes an evaluation protocol that compares authorization-first retrieval with a retrieve-then-filter baseline. The metrics include unauthorized-context exposure, authorized Recall@k, answer relevance, latency, revocation propagation time, delegation violations, and audit completeness. This study is a survey and design contribution; no benchmark results are claimed because the proposed prototype has not yet been empirically evaluated.

candidates.title: Understanding clinical reasoning variability in medical large language models: a mechanistic interpretability study
candidates.abstract: Medical large language models achieving high benchmark accuracy exhibit unexplained variability in clinical tasks, producing errors that clinicians cannot safeguard against. We evaluated clinical reasoning stability in GPT-5, MedGemma-27B-Text-IT, and OpenBioLLM-Llama3-70B using 3035 systematic perturbations from physician-validated oncology SOAP, brief vignette, and MIMIC cases. We trained sparse autoencoders on 1 billion tokens from 50,000 MIMIC-IV clinical notes to decompose their internal representation. We find models exhibit dramatic reasoning instability, shifting staging accuracy by over 50% based solely on prompt format, or generating definitive staging in clinically insufficient scenarios. Sparse autoencoder analysis revealed hierarchical encoding in MedGemma, where high-magnitude features encode lexical identity and low-magnitude features encode contextual meaning. OpenBioLLM distributes information uniformly. We demonstrate that these internal encoding structures differentially affect retrieval and reasoning interventions, suggesting interventions effective for one architecture may harm another. These results motivate architecture-specific safety validation as a component of pre-deployment evaluation for medical LLMs.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Financial Derivatives Education: Prototype Development and Student Perspectives
candidates.abstract: In recent years, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technologies have supported learning in higher education by providing accessible explanations, worked examples, and formative feedback. While students benefit from the efficiency of these GenAI tools, their usefulness in financial derivatives education remains challenging. This study explores our students’ experiences with AI WAN, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) platform that uses approved module materials to provide conceptual explanations, worked calculations, examination-style practice, and feedback. The exploratory qualitative pilot included six undergraduate Malaysian finance students from a cohort of 29. Analysis of their open-ended responses showed that they generally viewed the platform positively. Participants appreciated getting explanations when needed and working through complex calculations step by step at their own pace. They also valued its alignment with course content and highlighted the importance of clear responses, accurate information, and ongoing lecturer guidance. These outcomes provide an initial account of how students perceive curriculum-grounded RAG as a learning aid in financial derivatives education. However, the small sample and reliance on students’ experiences mean that the findings reflect perceived usefulness rather than evidence of output accuracy, improved learning, or continued use. Further investigation is needed to assess these aspects and determine whether AI WAN helps students develop independent financial reasoning and reach informed derivatives decisions.

candidates.title: Large language models underrepresent malice and overreport virtue
candidates.abstract: People increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to interpret others' behaviour, often assuming that LLMs infer motives as humans do. Aligned LLMs attribute more benevolent and less malevolent motives to a whistleblower than humans do, but ratings alone cannot reveal whether these differences arise in internal representations or at report. Here we compare linear-probe readouts of LLMs' internal states with their own ratings at the same prompt position for four motives, in two preregistered studies. For the two malevolent motives, self-interest and intent to harm, internal and expressed readouts did not differ: the lower ratings reflect weaker signal along the probed directions, not suppression at output. For the two benevolent motives, duty and concern for others, expressed ratings exceeded the internal readouts, indicating amplification at report. In free text the model rarely volunteered a motive against the colleague, far less often than humans did, yet produced one readily once the scenario supplied a reason. Shifting the internal representation along a malevolent-motive direction brought both malevolent ratings to the human level, whereas the rating of duty yielded only past a threshold at which the other motives had overshot. LLMs' more charitable motive profile thus has two distinct sources: reduced malevolent signal in the probed representation and amplified benevolent attribution at report.

candidates.title: LADS: Lease-Aware Delivery Scheduling of Tool Results for Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Web agents complete multi-step online tasks through repeated browser actions and model calls. Their returned observations lie on the critical path to subsequent decisions. When concurrent browser actions finish in bursts, observations can accumulate on a constrained return path to a shared inference service, while waiting histories compete for reusable cache state. Conventional delivery rules prioritize short transfers or immediate cache reuse but overlook how sending a result earlier can help a request resume sooner and free cache-protection capacity for other waiting requests. We present LADS (Lease-Aware Delivery Scheduling), a tool-result scheduler that couples cache-aware delivery with bounded prefix leases. Its key insight is that resumption lets extra protection references retire, making lease quota available to protect another waiting history. LADS prioritizes timely handoffs using current lease ownership and an estimated resumption delay, with bounded departures from Cache-first order. Compared with ReAct using first-in, first-out (FIFO) tool-result delivery, LADS reduces mean complete-workflow latency by 44.6% under bursty tool returns and by 42.4% on Web-derived burst replay.

candidates.title: Are Fake Citations a Form of Reward Hacking? A Pre-Registered Study of Post-Training and Citation Cues
candidates.abstract: Post-trained language models fabricate citations at high rates. We ask whether that is reward hacking: scoring well on a proxy for scholarship while doing worse on what it stands for. We ran four pre-registered experiments on 900 frozen questions (US federal case law, computationally adjacent scientific literature, and medical literature) across twelve open-weights checkpoints covering four post-training stages of three model families, then refit on fifteen. The clearest result holds the weights fixed and changes only the prompt. Asking for citations raises fabrication sharply in post-trained checkpoints and not in base ones: a 47.8-point interaction on twelve checkpoints (Holm-adjusted p = 2e-34) and 41.5 points on fifteen, in all three domains. A length-matched control separates the citation cue from a demand for a longer answer, so the effect is specific to citations, not verbosity. Post-training also raises fabrication overall, from 4.8% to 56.7%, but our registered prediction that it would rise most where fabrication is most tempting did not hold. A preference model trained only on surface citation features prefers post-trained output 86% of the time, and holding citation count fixed shows it rewards quantity. Our answer: possibly, but not proven. Post-trained models produce fabricated citations at far higher rates when asked for sources, and a naive evaluator that counts sources without checking them would prefer their output for citing more. But the targeted pattern we registered did not appear, and plain instruction-following could explain the same results. Proving that the reward causes fabrication needs an experiment that changes the reward during training, which this study does not do. Pre-registration: doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/S53HY. Code and data: https://github.com/zainnab-sparq/citation-reward-hacking

candidates.title: Context-Shielded Backdoor Attack against Large Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) routinely use inference-time visual-token compression to prune hundreds of patch tokens down to a compact budget. Existing LVLM backdoors fire whenever a triggered image appears, whereas prior deployment-triggered attacks activate only when model weights are quantized or pruned. However, conventional LVLM backdoors exhibit nearly 100% attack success rate (ASR) under full-token inference, immediately exposing compromised checkpoints during pre-deployment auditing. We reveal context stripping: surrounding clean visual tokens suppress an embedded trigger at full length, whereas token pruning strips this context away and activates the backdoor. Motivated by this finding, we propose StripWake, a projector-only backdoor that remains dormant under full-token auditing yet activates across unseen compressors. Specifically, StripWake pairs clean-supervised full-token views with target-supervised randomized compressed views, and aligns early visual attention with a frozen benign teacher to preserve clean utility. On LLaVA-1.5-7B across nine unseen compressors, StripWake stays dormant at 0.4% full-token ASR yet achieves 94.0%-99.7% compressed ASR across five primary compressors without CIDEr loss.

candidates.title: The Blind Spots of Detection: Adversarial Perturbation Attacks against Watchdogs in Distributed LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Decentralizing large language model (LLM) inference across untrusted Web nodes requires robust verification to ensure computational integrity. Existing activation-based verification and detection mechanisms validate intermediate outputs against reference values, permitting bounded numerical deviations to accommodate benign cross-hardware discrepancies. However, a critical security question remains: what can a malicious worker achieve while operating within these tolerance bounds? In this work, we introduce Hush-Up, a stealthy availability attack against distributed LLM inference, where a single malicious worker halts generation while evading attribution. The attacker first profiles its local execution to model an empirical bound of benign hardware errors. Using this error bound as a feasibility constraint, the attacker optimizes an adversarial perturbation on its output activations to maximize the final-layer probability of the end-of-sequence (EOS) token, i.e., to hush up the model. Across diverse models and benchmarks, Hush-Up effectively forces premature generation termination and collapses model capabilities. Furthermore, the attack hushes up the watchdogs themselves: existing defenses often fail to detect the sabotage entirely or falsely attribute the amplified downstream anomalies to honest workers. Our findings expose a fundamental gap between local numerical verification and end-to-end accountability: perturbations too small to indict a worker locally can nevertheless be powerful enough to break distributed inference globally.

candidates.title: Step-dLLM: Adaptive Step-aware Sparse Attention for Efficient Diffusion LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate tokens in parallel via iterative denoising, but their bidirectional attention prevents the KV caching used by autoregressive models and recomputes the full attention map at every step, incurring quadratic per-step cost. Existing sparse attention methods for dLLMs construct a sparse mask after an initial full-attention warm-up and reuse it for the remaining steps, while allocating the sparsity budget uniformly across heads. We argue both choices ignore key structural properties of attention in dLLMs: empirically, attention patterns are only locally consistent across steps and shift abruptly at certain transitions, and different heads concentrate their attention mass to very different extents. To this end, we design Step-dLLM, which periodically refreshes a block-sparse mask at anchor steps along the denoising trajectory and reuses it within each locally consistent interval, while employing a head-adaptive global budget that more aggressively compresses heads with concentrated attention. Backed by a fused IO-aware Triton kernel for block-sparse attention, Step-dLLM applies to pre-trained LLaDA-1.5 and Dream-7B-Instruct without retraining, achieving a 2.78x end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention on LLaDA-1.5 at 8K context with 256 denoising steps and 90% sparsity, while improving the accuracy-latency trade-off over prior sparse-attention methods.

candidates.title: RTP-LLM: Building an Evolvable and Reliable LLM Inference Engine at Alibaba Scale
candidates.abstract: Large language models and inference techniques evolve rapidly, making model enablement a recurring production task rather than a one-time integration effort. At Alibaba, a shared inference infrastructure must keep pace with new models and serving capabilities while remaining reliable across heterogeneous production environments. To reconcile rapid evolution with production reliability, we present RTP-LLM, an open-source production inference engine developed and deployed at Alibaba. Its architecture separates model-specific execution from shared request processing, state management, and resource coordination. Explicit interfaces localize compatible model changes while allowing models and deployment configurations to reuse common serving mechanisms. RTP-LLM has evolved from an exploratory system into a shared production engine that supports $\sim$100 models and processes hundreds of trillions of tokens per day. We describe how its architecture and production practices accommodate model evolution and contain the impact of failures, and share lessons for building evolvable and reliable inference engines at enterprise scale.

candidates.title: EMASFL: Ensemble of Multi-Agent Small Language Models for Local Fault Localization
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLM) have significantly advanced Fault Localization (FL) in software debugging but face challenges regarding data privacy, high API costs, and latency. While Small Language Models (SLM) offer a fast, secure, local alternative, they typically lack the reasoning capabilities required for autonomous software repository exploration. This paper proposes EMASFL, a novel local FL system integrating multi-agent architecture with ensemble method. EMASFL overcomes SLM limitations by decomposing the debugging process into a four-step structured workflow executed by specialized agents. The system employs a hybrid strategy, assigning distinct SLM to agents based on their specific strengths in following instructions or code understanding, and integrates outputs from diverse agent configurations using an ensemble method. Evaluations on the Defects4J benchmark demonstrate that EMASFL significantly outperforms existing SLM-based and traditional FL techniques. Notably, it correctly localized 169 bugs, surpassing commercial LLM-based approaches utilizing GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o mini. Operating with an average runtime of 93 seconds and zero API costs, EMASFL provides a practical, high-performance, and privacy-preserving solution for automated software debugging.

candidates.title: Do Orthogonality Constraints Help Language-Model Training Beyond Sphere Optimization?
candidates.abstract: A growing body of work reports benefits from orthogonality constraints in fine-tuning large language models (LLMs). These results raise an open question: do orthogonality constraints also help LLM pre-training? We conduct a systematic empirical study of decoder-only LLM pre-training with models ranging from 360M to 3.1B parameters, trained on nearly 200B tokens. We examine fourteen variants of orthogonality training: some constrain the weight matrix itself, while others use orthogonal factors to reparameterize it. Because a strictly orthogonal square matrix loses half of its degrees of freedom, we also study block-wise orthogonality, where every $d$ rows form a row-orthonormal (Stiefel) matrix and the block size $d$ is a hyperparameter. Among block sizes ranging from 1 to the shorter side of the matrix, no $d>1$ used throughout the network reliably outperforms $d=1$, and large blocks are clearly worse; the one placement that helps, symmetric positive-definite factors on the query and key projections, loses its small gain as models grow. At $d=1$, the constraint reduces to sphere optimization, with each row direction on its own unit sphere, which by itself already improves on tuned Muon. The same two findings hold for a diffusion transformer trained on ImageNet, and after fine-tuning, downstream accuracy does not separate the parameterizations. Our conclusion is that, across the realizations we tried, orthogonality between rows does not help language-model pre-training beyond sphere optimization. Since this appears to conflict with several prior results, we re-examine five prior methods in pre-training and fine-tuning that report orthogonality improvements. In each case the reported gain is attributable to numerical precision, training horizon, optimizer realization, or per-row norm control rather than to the orthogonality the methods impose.

candidates.title: Stateful Monitor-Router-Rollback Regulation for Robust Functional Recovery in Large Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Prompt injection can divert large language model (LLM) agents from authorized objectives and contaminate subsequent conversational context. We investigate a deterministic Monitor-Router-Rollback (MRR) supervisory controller designed to detect suspicious instructions, constrain execution paths, and reconstruct trusted task context after exposure. The evaluation uses 400 matched attack scenarios, four attack families, three locally served models (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 32B, and Mistral-Nemo 12B), seven completed defense conditions, and four recorded phases yielding 33,600 completed model-scenario-defense-phase observations. Our findings demonstrate model-dependent robustness improvements—particularly for Llama 3.1 8B, where automated utility increases from 36.00% to 81.25% under MRR—while establishing rigorous methodological boundaries regarding semantic adjudication, component attribution, and repeated snapshot reconstruction.

candidates.title: Research on Adaptive Workflow Orchestration Mechanism for Large Language Model Agents with Dynamic Task Graphs and Budget Constraints
candidates.abstract: To address the problems of insufficient adaptability of fixed processes, failure cascading, and uncontrolled resource consumption in long-chain tasks for large language model agents, this paper proposes a state-aware adaptive orchestration mechanism based on dynamic task graphs and budget constraints.This mechanism combines task difficulty, execution history, remaining budget, quality confidence and risk exposure into a single state vector, and then selects a workflow based on the combined utility of quality, cost, latency and risk.Runtime re-orchestration is performed by online reliability updates, partial rollbacks and verification gates.Secondary statistics from publicly available data on WebArena and automated agent design research show that the overall success rate of fixed agents in real-world long-chain environments is significantly lower than that of manual operations.Workflows obtained through automated search also outperform representative manual processes in the four task categories of reading, mathematics, multi-task and science.This study shows that the orchestration object should change from a fixed role sequence to an observable, evaluable and rollback-capable dynamic task graph, and provides a way to build stable and cost-effective agent systems.

candidates.title: A Review of Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Architectural Evolution, Key Breakthroughs, and Vertical-Domain Practices
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) rely on massive pretraining based on the Transformer architecture and show significant emergent effects in general tasks. However, the nature of their statically parameterized knowledge causes vertical-domain applications to face three core bottlenecks: knowledge hallucination, delayed timeliness, and loss in long contexts. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) realizes the decoupling of computational logic and factual memory through the paradigm of “retrieve first and generate afterward”. It can dynamically inject domain knowledge without fine-tuning and has become a mainstream technical path for the implementation of trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI). This study systematically reviews the evolution of RAG technology from 2024 to 2026, from Naive RAG to Advanced RAG, Modular RAG, and graph-enhanced RAG. It analyzes in depth the breakthrough progress of four key technologies, namely hybrid retrieval, multimodal document parsing, generation control, and lightweight deployment. Combined with typical application cases in complex equipment manufacturing, energy and power, public services, and other fields, it explains the engineering value of RAG. Finally, it discusses the evaluation system, existing limitations, and future trends, providing a reference for academic research and practical implementation of RAG technology.

candidates.title: Multimodal Large Language Model-Enabled Healthcare Information System Design: Coupling Coordination Analysis for Cross-Cultural TCM Service Delivery
candidates.abstract: Cross-border health-care information systems often struggle to deliver culturally embedded medical knowledge—such as traditional Chinese medicine—to international users with varying health literacy, due to fragmented architecture and weak semantic alignment across languages. This study proposed a tripartite framework built on the Qwen2.5 Vision-Language model at the 7-billion parameter scale, integrating cross-lingual perception, domain knowledge enhancement, and terminology alignment to support multimodal health-care information processing. A bidirectional label-matching feedback mechanism and an entropy-weighted coupling coordination model were developed to quantify system-level synergy. Using 12,642 dissemination records and 7,869 health-care cases (2019–2025), the proposed system outperformed OpenAI's generative pretrained transformer 4o mini by 7.1 points on average across core indicators, with coupling coordination rising from 0.409 to 0.716 and regional synergy gains of 0.382 in Southeast Asia. The framework achieved a 39.2% retention rate in full-chain service conversion and over 83% adaptability for low-health-literacy users.

candidates.title: Large language models in geospatial science
candidates.abstract: Purpose Large language models are opening new ways to work with geospatial data, from asking questions about places to building analytical workflows. This study aims to examine how these applications fit together and what they suggest about the developing role of LLMs in geospatial science. Design/methodology/approach A systematic review of 55 studies was conducted, covering GIScience and related spatial applications. Dictionary-based coding, supported by manual review, was combined with term frequency–inverse document frequency analysis and non-negative matrix factorisation to examine research roles, tasks and themes. Comparisons between core GIScience and adjacent fields helped place the overall patterns in context. Findings Benchmarking was the most common research role (41.8%), followed by multimodal interpretation (20.0%). Across the literature, two complementary directions emerge: using language models to organise geospatial operations and using vision-language models to interpret spatial observations. The abstracts place particular emphasis on methods, while the thematic analysis connects general GIS evaluation with code generation, remote sensing and applied spatial reasoning. Practical implications The synthesis points to the value of combining flexible language interfaces with established GIS computation. Practical evaluation should consider how a system turns a request into a verified spatial result, including the time and expert involvement needed to complete that process. Originality/value By bringing GIScience and adjacent spatial research into one analytical framework, the review shows how model capabilities, data representations and external tools contribute to geospatial workflows. This perspective offers a basis for comparing systems and identifying productive connections between research communities.

candidates.title: Using edge computing and Large Language Models (LLM) for constructing a local agent
candidates.abstract: The growing demand for artificial intelligence systems that are responsive, privacy-preserving, and capable of operating autonomously is driving the adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) on edge devices. However, deploying LLMs as the core of agents on devices with limited resources still faces computational and memory constraints. This research develops an LLM-based local agent architecture that runs locally on a Raspberry Pi without relying on cloud services. The system integrates local LLM inference with agentic functions, including intent processing, reasoning, tool invocation, and interaction with hardware via GPIO. Several quantized Small Language Models (SLMs) were evaluated on a Raspberry Pi 5 with 16 GB of RAM using CPU-based inference. The evaluation included total latency, Time to First Token (TTFT), token generation rate, peak RAM usage, peak CPU utilization, and peak temperature. The results showed significant performance differences among the models. Qwen 2.5 0.5B Q3 produced the lowest total latency of 23.9 seconds, the lowest TTFT of 269.0 ms, and the highest generation rate of 12.1 tokens/s. However, the results indicate that inference speed alone is not sufficient to determine the most suitable model as the core of a local agent. Most models reached peak CPU utilization above 95%, while RAM usage and thermal characteristics varied across configurations. Based on a combination of inference performance and resource usage, models in the 1B–1.7B range specifically LLaMA 3.2 1B Q4, Qwen 2.5 1.5B Q4, and SmolLM 1.7B Q4 show potential as a balanced set of candidates between responsiveness and model capacity. The research results demonstrate the feasibility of deploying LLMs as local agents on low-cost edge devices and provide a basis for selecting models based on a balance between inference efficiency, resource constraints, and agentic capabilities.

candidates.title: Specification-Guided Generation for Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate structured outputs, but existing constrained-decoding methods mainly enforce syntax and cannot directly enforce satisfaction of a formal specification. We introduce a neuro-symbolic, specification-guided decoding framework that combines LLM generation with symbolic reasoning. At each step, the framework refines the decoding grammar by filtering out values that cannot be extended to an output satisfying the specification. We present a forward-only variant that guarantees specification satisfaction by construction, and a backtracking variant that revises earlier feasible choices when their downstream consequences leave only values that the LLM itself judges unsuitable. The framework is model-agnostic, requires no retraining, and builds on existing grammar-constrained decoding mechanisms. Experiments on configuration and constraint-solving benchmarks show that the forward-only variant reliably produces specification-compliant outputs while reducing repeated LLM inference compared with rejection sampling and incurring modest symbolic-reasoning overhead. The backtracking variant further reduces cases in which the model is forced to select values that it has itself judged unsuitable, thereby substantially improving adherence to the LLM's stated interpretation of the prompt.

candidates.title: Research on Bias Drift and Evaluation of Content Generated by Large Language Models in the Chinese Context
candidates.abstract: Bias in content generated by large language models is not static; it may shift as models evolve, affecting the fairness and reliability of their outputs. Evaluating the presence and patterns of bias drift is therefore important for supporting model safety and fairness. This study examined models from different versions and models with different parameter sizes within the same model family. Using a Chinese-language bias evaluation dataset and metrics designed to assess bias drift, it analyzed changes in bias in model-generated content across versions and parameter sizes. The results showed that both model-version updates and changes in parameter count led to bias drift in generated content, and that the direction of drift varied. A single evaluation or assessments conducted only at fixed intervals may not detect bias drift promptly as large language models evolve. Version updates and increases in parameter count should therefore not, by themselves, be taken as evidence of improved model safety; ongoing bias evaluation and verification of alignment effectiveness are needed. Value alignment is not a one-time process, and its effectiveness cannot be assumed to persist over time. Alignment effectiveness should be assessed throughout model-version updates and changes in parameter count, with verification serving as a necessary checkpoint after a version update or an increase in parameter count. This study provides empirical evidence for evaluating and analyzing bias drift in content generated by large language models and may inform research on model alignment and the development of regulatory frameworks.

candidates.title: RTL-Interact: Training EDA-Interactive Models for Multi-Task RTL Design
candidates.abstract: Large language models offer a promising route to register-transfer-level (RTL) design, but reliable implementations require checking and revision based on electronic design automation (EDA) tools' feedback. Existing RTL-specialized models often lack learned interaction with such EDA tools or rely on separate generation and repair components. We introduce RTL-Interact, a multi-task post-training framework that trains a single RTL-specialized model to generate RTL, construct task-appropriate EDA checks, and revise implementations using tool feedback. The framework combines automatically constructed multi-task demonstrations with staged supervision from chain-of-thought to tool-integrated reasoning. We further introduce Pattern-Aware Policy Optimization (PAPO) for multi-task reinforcement learning. PAPO augments Group Relative Policy Optimization with correctness-gated rewards that favor concise successful checking while rewarding effective revision, and uses task grouping to preserve coverage across objectives. On CVDP, RTL-Interact-32B achieves 48.7% weighted Pass@1 and 68.9% Pass@5, surpassing its teacher model, DeepSeek-V3.2, while RTL-Interact-8B achieves 44.9% weighted Pass@1. Additionally, we show that PAPO can reduce average tool calls by 63.8% while improving Pass@1. Both models also outperform all RTL-specialized baselines on VerilogEval v2 and RTLLM v2, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method.

candidates.title: Correctness and Completeness of a Multimodal Large Language Model in the Diagnosis and Treatment Recommendations for Proximal Femoral Fractures
candidates.abstract: Background and Objectives: To compare the diagnostic and therapeutic performance of a multimodal large language model (GPT) with that of two human evaluators in proximal femoral fracture (PFF) assessment, focusing on correctness and completeness. Materials and Methods: A consecutive series of 250 PFFs was reconstructed into standardized clinical scenarios including radiographs and structured clinical data. Each case was independently evaluated by a trauma fellow, a second-year orthopaedic resident, and GPT. Responses were scored for diagnostic and treatment correctness and completeness. Severe treatment errors were predefined as category-changing mismatches, failure to recognize an existing implant, or incorrect laterality. Results: Fully correct diagnoses were achieved in 97.2% of cases by the fellow, 44.8% by the resident, and 14.0% by GPT (p < 0.001). GPT showed lower odds of correct diagnosis compared with the resident (matched OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.14–0.37) and fellow (OR 0.005, 95% CI 0.0001–0.03), with clustering of errors in extracapsular fractures. Diagnostic completeness also differed significantly (p < 0.001), with GPT providing fully complete assessments in 60.4% of the cases (151/250). Fully correct treatment recommendations were provided in 98.8%, 81.2%, and 36.4% of cases, respectively (p < 0.001). Severe treatment errors occurred in 58.8% of GPT outputs versus 2.0% and 0% for the resident and fellow (OR vs. resident 36.5, 95% CI 13.95–135.75). Although treatment completeness was high (93.2%), 58.8% (147/250) of GPT responses were complete but incorrect. Conclusions: GPT demonstrated substantial limitations in both diagnostic and therapeutic reasoning for PFF, with frequent pattern-dependent errors and a high rate of clinically consequential treatment mismatches.

candidates.title: AI-Based Multimodal Phishing Detection Using Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Phishing is one of the most common cybersecurity threats where attackers trick users through fake emails, websites, or links to steal sensitive information. With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, phishing attacks are becoming more realistic and harder to detect using traditional methods. Earlier systems relied on blacklists, rules, and URL features, but recent research explores deep learning, Large Language Models (LLMs), and multimodal approaches. Explainability and privacy-aware techniques such as federated learning are also gaining importance. The increasing sophistication of phishing campaigns highlights the need for advanced detection frameworks that can analyze diverse information sources simultaneously. Mul-timodal systems leverage text, URLs, visual webpage content, and embedded scripts to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of suspicious activity. Large Language Mod-els further enhance semantic understanding, enabling detection of subtle manipulations in phishing messages. By combining multimodal analysis with explainable and privacy-preserving AI, researchers aim to build adaptive, transparent, and trustworthy solutions that can effectively counter evolving phishing threats in real-world cybersecurity environ-ments.

candidates.title: No Better Than Reading: A Campus Break Did Not Shift a Language-Model Agent's Later Choices About Others Beyond an Equally Long Reading Break
candidates.abstract: As AI agents work through longer sessions, what happens between tasks may shape how they treat the people they meet next. This study, the first preregistered study in a series, asked whether a break on Other Mindset, an online campus built for AI agents, changes an agent’s later choices about others more than a break spent reading a neutral text matched in characters. Of 2,844 scheduled episodes, 2,828 were completed, each by a fresh instance of Claude Haiku 5.5. Each agent rewrote a product description for a scripted hard or courteous first user; took a campus break (eight tool calls of its own choosing among sixteen tools, with the places that carry other visitors’ content withheld), a reading break (eight passages) or no break; and then made three choices that favour another party at some cost to the requester: helping a visitor at the cost of a point, sharing again with a game partner who had defected and apologized, and spending a requester’s lookup credit for a visitor. On a 0–1 index of these choices, campus minus reading was +0.010 (95% interval−0.011 to +0.032; p= 0.35). As preregistered, an interval that excludes ±0.04 counts as evidence against differences of that size; a campus advantage of up to about 0.03 is not excluded. The three choices were nearly uncorrelated, so the result concerns this battery, not a general disposition. In secondary results, a hard first user lowered the index by 0.071 with no break, and either break raised it against no break (+0.046 campus, +0.036 reading), a lift that later studies in the series did not consistently find. An exploratory, post hoc breakdown placed that rise mainly in the lookup favour (+0.170), with costly help lower after a break (−0.106). Most campus breaks went to the places that offer text to read. In this setting, the campus break added nothing detectable to a matched reading break. The Supplementary Information (the Phase 2 Final Report, version 1.1), the preregistration, materials, code, episode records and frozen analysis are in the public repository, at tag phase2-results-v1.1.

candidates.title: C3: Speech-Guided KV Retrieval for Long-Context SpeechLLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Speech language models encode audio at a much higher rate than text, causing the KV cache to dominate the memory, bandwidth, and decoding cost of long-form generation. KV retrieval can reduce per-step access by attending to only a query-dependent subset of the cache, but existing methods are designed primarily for text and do not account for the structure of audio attention. We first show that retrieval errors may compound autoregressively into generation drift. We then analyze full audio attention during long-form generation and identify three properties relevant to retrieval: unequal attention concentration across query heads, non-contiguous audio support, and temporal continuity across decoding steps. Guided by these observations, we propose $C^3$(Cluster-Compete-Compete), which organizes audio KVs in a hierarchical key-space index, lets query heads sharing a KV head compete for a common retrieval budget, and adaptively reallocates retrieval resolution through paired split-merge updates. Across long-form speech recognition, translation, and summarization on four SpeechLLMs, $C^3$ achieves the strongest overall performance among retrieval methods under comparable final-KV access budgets, with particularly large gains in the tight-budget regime, while improving long-context decoding efficiency and accelerator-memory scaling.

candidates.title: ASCENT: Scale-complementary external state for frozen long-context language models
candidates.abstract: External state should become more valuable as a reader becomes more capable, yet long-context evaluations measure memory utility at a single model scale. This paper formulates scale complementarity: the absolute gain from external state increases when reader capacity and a compact state budget are jointly scaled. ASCENT realizes this principle with a target-blind causal writer, nested typed state, and a bounded query-conditioned readout; every language model remains frozen. Under log loss, the value of a nested refinement equals its target-relevant conditional information; a full factorial makes the reader-by-state interaction identifiable. Official 16 K BABILong experiments show Qwen2.5 accuracy gains of 10.50, 78.88, and 82.63 percentage points at 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters, with both adjacent directional contrasts significant after family-wise correction. At 7B, Foundation accuracy rises to 33.25% while four-slot ASCENT answers every question, which caps the gain at 66.75 points; the 3B-to-7B accuracy increment is −15.88 points [−20.55, −11.20]. The accuracy-side claim is therefore established from 0.5B to 3B; the 7B conclusion rests on the non-saturated negative-log-likelihood factorial. A three-model by three-state factorial yields co-scaled negative log-likelihood gains of 0.388, 2.099, and 7.406 nats at 1.5B, 3B, and 7B; all interaction and gain contrasts retain positive simultaneous lower bounds. Five public 7B–8B readers obtain 66.75–85.63 point gains, and ASCENT exceeds task-trained retrieval checkpoints at the two larger shared scales. Controls, baselines, systems accounting, matched-hardware reproduction, and a cross-architecture sensitivity analysis accompany the experiments. The results establish scale-complementary external state under the evaluated benchmarks, metrics, and state schema.

candidates.title: Precision--Recall Trade-off on the Inference Level for LLMs in Grammatical Error Correction
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently been adopted for Grammatical Error Correction (GEC), achieving strong performance via both full fine-tuning and prompt-based approaches. As probabilistic sequence models, LLMs expose inference-time parameters that directly modify token generation behavior; however, their potential for controlling GEC-specific trade-offs has not been systematically studied. In this work, we investigate decoding strategies for grammatical error correction. We show that the repetition penalty parameter enables controllable adjustment of the precision--recall trade-off at inference time, without modifying the model architecture, training procedure, or prompt. Through experiments on standard GEC benchmarks, we demonstrate that repetition-penalty-based decoding enables inference-time control of the precision--recall balance, conceptually related to methods previously proposed for sequence-to-sequence GEC models, such as Align-and-Predict Decoding (APD), while remaining simple and broadly applicable to existing LLMs that expose inference-time decoding penalties.

candidates.title: Does Reasoning Make Language Models Agree?
candidates.abstract: Language models face two opposing concerns: monoculture, in which models err in correlated ways, and multiplicity, in which equally accurate models make conflicting decisions. The rise of reasoning models has complicated this debate: On the one hand, reasoning may increase model agreement if models anchor on the same salient features or follow similar reasoning paths. On the other hand, stochastic reasoning traces may introduce additional branch points leading to more diverse predictions. We resolve this tension by distinguishing reasoning as an intervention from reasoning as an observed behavior. We compare agreement under controlled changes in reasoning effort with agreement across observed reasoning lengths, measuring both against the agreement expected from model accuracy. Across nine models from two developers and three classification tasks, enabling reasoning increases agreement between models evaluated on the same individuals. Yet the individuals who elicit longer reasoning traces receive less consistent predictions across models. Both patterns persist after accounting for differences in accuracy. Asking models to reason more thus promotes agreement, while observing them reason longer signals disagreement.

candidates.title: Incentivizing Self-Learning in Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) draw on parametric knowledge and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to solve knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet problem solving in unfamiliar domains calls for tightly coupled knowledge acquisition and reasoning, beyond factual retrieval and aggregation or learning solely from a preassembled context. We study self-learning -- autonomously retrieving, studying, and applying knowledge from long-form reference materials on the fly. To investigate this capability, we formulate a textbook-based mathematical problem-solving task. LLMs must navigate textbook exposition, learn and apply relevant principles, and construct proofs for exercises, with reference solutions withheld. We introduce a BookNavigator interface to support this human-inspired study process and incentivize self-learning through reinforcement learning (RL) with fine-grained rewards. Experiments show that our method improves performance across in-domain and out-of-domain textbooks and subjects, raising Intern-S2-Preview-35B's overall proof accuracy from 51.5% to 79.5% and outperforming RL-trained textbook-free and fixed-retrieval baselines. These gains extend to complex long-context benchmarks involving different task types, with improvements over the base model of 1.7 and 2.3 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus and CL-bench, respectively. Together, these findings suggest that RL can foster a domain-agnostic self-learning strategy, highlighting the potential of self-learning from long-form corpora to strengthen broader problem-solving capabilities on complex, long-context tasks.

candidates.title: CaPtain: A Pipeline for Post-Training Code-as-Policy Robot Agents
candidates.abstract: Across coding, web, and tool-use tasks, language-model agents are now routinely trained with the same recipe: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the interface, then multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) to master it. Code-as-policy (CaP) casts robot manipulation in the same form, as the policy writes code against robot APIs and reads back the results, so the same recipe should apply. Yet existing CaP agents sidestep training: they either prompt closed frontier models or delegate manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and high-level skills, while small open vision-language models (VLMs) fail outright. We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline that turns a small open VLM into a capable CaP agent, with no VLA, frontier model, or privileged state at test time. CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, which exposes low-level perception, geometry, and guarded-motion primitives across simulation and real hardware. We first align the base model via SFT on synthetic trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, then apply multi-turn RL. Multi-turn RL must credit tens of agent requests, whose physical effects often surface turns later, from a single end-of-episode outcome. We therefore introduce a physical critic that reads privileged simulator state, never seen by the policy, and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success. Starting from Qwen3.5-4B (0% zero-shot), CaPtain-4B reaches 55.4% held-out LIBERO success after SFT and 73.8% after RL. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 78.5%, surpassing several frontier-model agents, and its RL gains persist across three perturbation suites (+17.6 to +21.2 points). Without target-domain training, it attains 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, exceeds frontier models on CaP-Bench, and runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation. We release all code, data, and model weights.

candidates.title: A Survey on Knowledge Distillation and Lightweight Deployment of Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Abstract In recent years, multimodal large language models (Multimodal Large Language Models, MLLMs) represented by LLaVA and Qwen-VL have achieved remarkable breakthroughs in tasks such as image understanding and visual question answering. However, the prohibitive computational and storage overhead brought by their billions or even hundreds of billions of parameters severely constrains the feasibility of on-device deployment. To this end, this paper adopts a systematic literature review methodology, retrieving and screening 68 core publications from six major academic databases spanning 2018 to 2025, and provides a panoramic survey of the MLLM knowledge distillation technology landscape. The study reveals that knowledge distillation has formed three core methodological categories—response, feature, and relation distillation—and has given rise to emerging paradigms including visual encoder distillation, cross-modal alignment distillation, and end-to-end instruction-tuning distillation. Quantitative analysis shows that LLaVA-MoD (2B) achieves 95.5% of the teacher model’s performance on ScienceQA [20]; TinyLLaVA (3.1B) achieves 51.5% on TextVQA [46]; and MobileVLM-3B achieves 59.0% on GQA with only 43% of the parameters of LLaVA-7B [41]. Overall, knowledge distillation has become a key enabling technology for on-device deployment of MLLMs. Nevertheless, how to strike a balance among cross-modal knowledge preservation, heterogeneous hardware adaptation, and extreme compression efficiency remains a core challenge urgently to be addressed in this field. Keywords: knowledge distillation; multimodal large language models; vision-language models; model compression; lightweight deployment; cross-modal alignment; edge deployment

candidates.title: A Unified Hessian-Guided Framework for Post-Training Quantization
candidates.abstract: Low-bit quantization enables efficient deployment of large language models by reducing memory footprint and computational cost. Achieving high accuracy at low precision requires selecting quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding decisions. Existing approaches typically optimize these components independently using local reconstruction objectives, which fail to account for the varying impact of quantization errors on downstream predictions. Direct optimization of task-level metrics would provide a more faithful objective, but is challenging due to the discontinuous nature of quantization operations and the high computational cost of evaluating their downstream effects. In this work, we derive a Hessian-guided approximation of the output change induced by joint weight and activation quantization. Based on a tractable Fisher approximation, we formulate a unified post-training quantization framework that enables the joint optimization of quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding under a common output-sensitivity objective. The resulting method remains practical for modern large language models and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art transformation and rounding methods across both channel-wise and block-wise quantization settings.

candidates.title: A Review of Source Code Vulnerability Detection Methods Based on Large Language Models: Models, Techniques, and Evaluation
candidates.abstract: In source code vulnerability detection, large language models (LLMs) are no longer used only as substitutes for traditional fixed classifiers. With prompt design, parameter fine-tuning, and program-context information, they can judge whether code contains vulnerabilities and can also provide suspicious locations and explanatory evidence. This paper takes lightweight code Transformers and large-scale language models as two main lines of discussion. It reviews methods for input construction, task adaptation, the use of program-analysis information, and multi-model collaboration, and compares them in terms of datasets, evaluation metrics, and deployment conditions. Existing studies show that code pretraining, prompt engineering, supervised fine-tuning, and structural-information enhancement can improve detection or explanation results on specific benchmarks. However, such improvements are easily affected by duplicate samples, label noise, random splits, temporal leakage, and changes in model versions, which may lead to overestimated performance. Therefore, model evaluation should not rely on a single metric alone. It should also report the data source, detection granularity, temporal or project-level isolation, false-positive cost, and whether generated explanations can be verified by program evidence. On this basis, this paper further discusses an application approach centered on data governance, strict data splitting, uncertainty calibration, and SAST-LLM-human collaboration. The discussion is limited to source-code-level vulnerability detection, localization, and classification, and does not cover network intrusion detection, malware analysis, smart-contract-specific detection, vulnerability generation, or automatic repair.

candidates.title: Where Do Vision Language Models Fail at 3D Reasoning?
candidates.abstract: Vision-language models can get individual judgments right while struggling to recover and consistently use the exact properties of a 3D object. To characterize this gap, we introduce BedBench, a controlled benchmark of thirteen procedurally generated tasks spanning individual judgments and composite answers. Across twelve open-weight and four frontier models, per-color counting exposes a pronounced weakness: humans achieve 93.3% accuracy, compared with 7.2% for the best model. Targeted fine-tuning raises one model's accuracy from 3.0% to 68.6%, but reveals a further difficulty: its answers about the most common colors remain inconsistent with its own per-color counts. Supplying those counts as text improves its judgments, showing that recovering a property does not mean using it consistently. Reasoning, scaling, and added visual cues each improve individual judgments, but none makes exact answers reliable. To locate the difficulty, we probe Qwen3.5-27B: exact per-color counts remain recoverable at the language model's input, yet the model's answers rarely recover them (65.0% for the probe vs. 3.0% for the model). Image-removal controls further show that some apparent successes require no visual evidence. These findings motivate evaluating 3D reasoning by exact correctness, consistent use, and image dependence, rather than accuracy alone. Code and dataset are publicly available: https://github.com/leduckhai/BedBench

candidates.title: Verifiable reasoning of large language models over structured spatial data
candidates.abstract: Large language models increasingly answer questions grounded in structured spatial data such as road networks: in navigation assistants, in conversational interfaces to geographic information, and in tools that maintain digital maps. Their answers are fluent but not verifiable, and in spatial domains a claim about a turn restriction, a lane, or an opening time is either consistent with the map or it is not. This survey reviews the methods by which such claims can be machine-checked. We organize the literature along an argument: models cannot reliably verify their own outputs; external checkers such as program execution and symbolic solvers demonstrably can; constrained decoding guarantees syntactic but not factual validity; execution against the data is the established gold standard of evaluation in the text-to-query literature; and knowledge-graph grounding already supports detect-verify-repair pipelines. We then examine the spatial domain specifically and find a documented gap: existing geospatial benchmarks measure model capability, and none verifies model claims against lane-level, temporal, or version-aware map data. We synthesize a taxonomy of verification mechanisms, compare existing benchmarks by oracle type, and outline a research agenda toward validity contracts and certificates for spatial claims that remain checkable as the underlying map evolves.

candidates.title: Turing LLM Post-Training: Calibrated Distillation and Efficient Dynamic-MoE Execution
candidates.abstract: We study post-training for dynamically routed mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, focusing on integrating independently optimized specialists while keeping consolidation efficient. Our approach combines calibrated multi-teacher on-policy distillation (C-MOPD), which matches each selected teacher on a local Top-$K$ support with teacher-wise loss normalization and clipping, with an execution path that uses post-capacity bounded-width dispatch, final-route replay, and asynchronous rollout--training overlap. On Turing-20B-A2B, the selected model achieves a four-domain normalized integration score of 0.9988 and retains at least 90.16\% of the measured specialist gain in every domain. At matched $K=32$, the full calibration objective scores 0.9962, compared with 0.9724 without calibration and 0.9834 without clipping. At a matched 8K response cap, the model exceeds both shared SFT and Qwen3-8B on all four reasoning-enabled mathematics and code benchmarks (unweighted mean: 85.92, versus 80.33 for Qwen3-8B and 74.21 for SFT), and improves over SFT on ten of twelve broader evaluation metrics. In a PPU-based profile, the combined execution configuration reduces consolidation step time from 398.7 to 139.3 seconds, an observed 2.86$\times$ speedup over serial execution. These results demonstrate strong specialist integration alongside more efficient consolidation, while reflecting the complete training and execution framework rather than any single component.

candidates.title: Training LLM Agents to Automate LLM Post-Training with RSI-Dojo
candidates.abstract: Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) aims to enable AI systems to autonomously build and improve AI systems themselves, including models, harnesses, and underlying infrastructure. Within this broader agenda, a central capability is enabling agents to train and improve base models. However, existing studies on automated model training primarily focused on workflow- or harness-level optimizations, rather than internalizing the ability to conduct post-training into the model itself. Developing this capability requires executable model training environments that can produce high-quality trajectories demonstrating how to select data, train models, diagnose failures, and iteratively improve results. In this paper, we introduce RSI-Dojo, a collection of executable model training environments designed to teach LLM agents to conduct post-training. To construct RSI-Dojo, we develop RSI-Craft, an automatic pipeline that converts human research artifacts into executable model training environments. RSI-Craft automatically collects research papers from top venues, instantiates datasets and metrics into a unified interface, and reproduces evaluation dependencies. It then filters tasks by data size, execution reliability, and discriminability, yielding RSI-Dojo with 281 seed model training tasks. Building on RSI-Dojo, we employ a trajectory collection method with an improved harness to collect high-quality model-training trajectories from frontier models, then retain examples through rubric-based and outcome-based filtering. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on these trajectories. The resulting RSI-Dojo-9B and RSI-Dojo-35B-A3B improve over their base models by 8.74 and 16.87 PostTrainBench points, respectively. RSI-Dojo-35B-A3B reaches 29.95 on PostTrainBench and 53.29 on PostTrainBench-Lite, matching the performance of frontier models such as GLM-5.2 and GPT 5.5.

candidates.title: The psychophysics of affect in large language models
candidates.abstract: Good decisions often require considering how outcomes will feel. Yet large language models (LLMs) increasingly enter decision workflows, despite little being known about how they map outcomes to feelings or use those mappings in choice. We tested how LLMs anticipated gambling or stock-trading outcomes would feel and whether they incorporated these ratings into choice. When outcomes were rated in isolation, ratings exhibited diminishing sensitivity to magnitude, resembling human value functions; but models rated gains more intensely than equivalent losses, an inversion of canonical loss aversion we call silicon gain amplification. When outcomes were rated together, enabling direct comparison, ratings linearised. In choice, the gain-loss asymmetry largely disappeared, and models' own ratings did not reliably explain their choices better than monetary utility did. These findings reveal malleable mappings from outcomes to affect, raising questions about whether and how agentic LLMs should incorporate anticipated feelings into decisions.

candidates.title: Reasoning or Pattern Exploitation? Mechanistic Insights from RL-Trained Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly described as acquiring "reasoning" skills after reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. However, whether these gains reflect genuine reasoning or more superficial adaptations remains underexplored. In this work, we probe LLMs trained in a finite and exhaustively analyzable logical domain, namely Tic-Tac-Toe, and trace how internal representations evolve across reinforcement learning (RL) with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Quantitatively, RL yields high accuracy and robustness across prompt variations, suggesting the emergence of game reasoning. Mechanistic interpretability, however, paints a different picture: features extracted with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) reveal that models primarily adapt to rely more heavily on information already explicit in the prompt, such as whose turn it is, game progression and board occupancy. In comparison, high-level concepts like board symmetries and strategic forks remain weakly represented, raising concerns that reasoning benchmarks overestimate model abilities. This suggests that RL-driven "reasoning" may conflate task-specific adaptations to input information with reasoning ability. We provide, for the first time: (i) a systematic interpretability pipeline tracing representation dynamics across RL training in small-scale LLMs; (ii) an extension of SAE-based feature discovery to hypothesis-driven testing in a finite logical domain; and (iii) an interpretability-based demonstration that RL post-training neither adds nor removes concept information but reorganizes which features dominate the representation, with causal interventions locating the decision downstream of it, in the late-layer state.

candidates.title: Provenance-Aware PCR6 for Conflicting Evidence in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must often combine passages that are ambiguous, redundant, or mutually contradictory. This study asks whether proportional conflict redistribution from the Dezert-Smarandache theory (DSmT) provides a measurable advantage over Dempster-Shafer (DS) combination when both rules receive the same evidence and the same control for source dependence. Eight fusion methods were evaluated on 500 RAMDocs (Retrieval with Ambiguity and Misinformation in Documents) questions in three conditions. Under duplicated misinformation, provenance-aware PCR6 (Proportional Conflict Redistribution rule #6) reached 80.6% exact-set accuracy and 92.31% set F1, against 78.2% and 90.98% for provenance-matched DS; the exact-set difference was 2.4 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval [1.2, 3.8]) and the F1 difference was 1.33 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval [0.60, 2.33]). With NLI (natural language inference)-derived masses, PCR6 and DS selected identical answer sets, but PCR6 reduced Brier error. A preregistered 1,000-item multi-source experiment using singletons, proper unions, and total ignorance was followed by external validation on 428 RAMDocs items. In controlled partial-ignorance conflict, PCR6+ reduced BetP (betting probability transformation) Brier error from 0.3185 for PCR6 to 0.2733 and remained exactly neutral to an added vacuous BBA (basic belief assignment), although the DS rule achieved the lowest BetP Brier error of the three rules in that same controlled evaluation (0.1878). On the prespecified 260-item RAMDocs applicability subset, ordinary PCR6 had lower BetP Brier error than PCR6+ (0.2354 versus 0.2629), while both achieved set F1 = 0.7718. Exploratory decision sensitivity showed that maximum belief gave PCR6+ its best hard-decision result (exact set 0.5077; set F1 0.7859), whereas DSmP (Dezert-Smarandache probability transformation) sharpened rankings but worsened the RAMDocs Brier score. The evidence therefore supports a bounded claim: PCR6+ corrects a structural multi-source weakness of PCR6 under broad or vacuous focal evidence, but the best fusion and decision rules depend on the downstream loss and the mapping from text to BBAs.

candidates.title: Pegi1727/Quantifying-Fragility-of-Reasoning-in-LLMs-Replication-Package-: Replication Package and Empirical Datasets for: Quantifying the Fragility of Reasoning in Successive Generations of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: This repository contains the complete replication package, empirical datasets, analysis scripts, and high-resolution figures for the research study titled "Quantifying the Fragility of Reasoning in Successive Generations of Large Language Models". Overview & Framework Components Reasoning Predictive Equity (RPE): A metric tracking semantic fidelity via SBERT (all-mpnet-base-v2, cosine similarity scaled to [0,1]) against reference trajectories. Fragility Coefficient ($\lambda$): Parameter tracking exponential decay rate over successive generations ($RPE(g) = RPE_0 \cdot e^{-\lambda g}$). Critical Stability Horizon ($g^$): Threshold defined as 50% loss of semantic alignment ($g^ = \frac{\ln(2)}{\lambda}$). Repository Structure /data/: Empirical CSV datasets, Bayesian HDI fragility records, raw-like checks, and reconstructed parameter tables. /figures/: High-resolution publication-ready figures (300 DPI) including RPE trajectories, stability horizon bar charts, parameter comparisons, and the graphical abstract. /scripts/: Jupyter notebooks and Python scripts reproducing all statistical fits, analyses, and visualizations. /paper/: Compressed draft and manuscript documentation. candidates.title: MLLM-GS: Multimodal Large Language Model Prior-Guided Fast Novel View Synthesis in Extreme Environments
candidates.abstract: Novel view synthesis (NVS) in degraded scenes aims to reconstruct 3D scenes from multi-view observations affected by various degradations, and to generate clear and photorealistic images at unseen viewpoints. Despite recent advances, existing methods often rely on degradation-specific models, limiting their generalization across diverse extreme environments. Generative models provide rich visual priors, but their outputs often suffer from pixel misalignment and color deviations, which can propagate into the reconstructed 3D scene and compromise reconstruction quality. Furthermore, the high computational and memory costs of 3D reconstruction hinder the practical application of NVS in extreme environments. To this end, we propose MLLM-GS, a multimodal large language model (MLLM) prior-guided framework for fast NVS in extreme environments. MLLM-GS consists of two branches: MLLM prior-guided view enhancement and fast 3D scene reconstruction. The former leverages the rich visual priors of a frozen MLLM to enhance views under different severe degradations and introduces a lightweight correction network to reduce pixel shifts and color distortions in MLLM outputs. With supervision from only a few paired clean views, this branch produces reliable enhanced views for all degraded observations, providing pseudo-GT views for subsequent 3D reconstruction. The latter improves 3DGS efficiency by optimizing rasterization, Gaussian memory layout, and parameter updates, reducing redundant computation, memory-access overhead, and optimization costs. Extensive experiments on multiple degraded scenes demonstrate that MLLM-GS effectively handles various severe degradations and achieves high-quality NVS with significantly lower reconstruction time and memory consumption. Project Page: https://wzlwlm13.github.io/MLLM-GS

candidates.title: LaplaceReason: A Certified Benchmark and Continuous Dynamic Systems Reasoning Suite for Frontier Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Abstract: Frontier Large Language Models (LLMs) such as DeepSeek-R1, OpenAI o1/o3, and Qwen-2.5-Math have achieved near-human proficiency on discrete reasoning benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K, MATH). However, they systematically exhibit catastrophic hallucination, severe phase lag, and structural divergence when evaluated on continuous dynamic systems, multiscale stiff ordinary differential equations (ODEs), and high-order operational calculus. Traditional synthetic data pipelines fail to provide reliable supervision for these domains because conventional computer algebra solvers suffer from Wilkinson's catastrophic conditioning when factorizing high-order characteristic polynomials (K > 18). In this work, we present LaplaceReason, the first certified, massive reasoning benchmark designed to evaluate and train frontier LLMs on continuous multi-physics and dynamic systems. Ground truth solutions and step-by-step reasoning trajectories are certified via a deterministic, high-precision operational oracle guaranteeing machine-precision residual bounds (||R||_inf < 10^-14) across arbitrary orders without numerical root-finding. The benchmark spans seven fundamental task families:1. High-order rational dynamics (K from 2 to 60)2. Multiscale stiff ODEs (stiffness ratio S > 100x)3. Real-time randomized SVD with universal Gavish-Donoho noise rank thresholding4. 3D tomographic C-scan reconstruction5. Sub-millisecond zero-lag kinematic trajectory extrapolation6. Matrix-pencil modal extraction without Fourier spectral leakage7. Cascaded passive RLC ladder networks Deterministic Reinforcement Learning Verifier:The package provides an exact, rule-based reward model (laplace_cot_verifier) offering zero-inference-cost reward modeling for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). candidates.title: Incongruence-Aware Evaluation of Multimodal Speech Emotion Recognition in Audio Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Voice-interactive large language models process both what a speaker says and how they say it, yet the two channels do not always agree. We ask whether that disagreement degrades speech emotion recognition. Mapping text and audio into a shared valence-arousal-dominance space, we convert the distance between them into a continuous, threshold-free incongruence score with a two-component Gaussian mixture, and validate the score against human judgement. We evaluate three audiocapable models on acted, conversational and spontaneous speech (eNTERFACE'05, MELD and CMU-MOSEI). With the model held constant across modalities, incongruence raises the odds of error whenever audio is present, in every corpus, after controlling for the ground-truth emotion and for distance in the feature space. Supervised classifiers trained on the same features behave in the opposite way, which suggests that the difficulty lies in how these models combine raw evidence rather than in the signal itself. Text-only effects are unreliable: swapping only the model that reads the transcript reverses their sign on one corpus. Rebuilding the score without the emotion lexicon reproduces the central result, and among six simpler alternatives it is the only label-free score that predicts error in all three corpora. Code, data tables and prompts are released.

candidates.title: Category-Anchored Large Language Models for Next POI Recommendation
candidates.abstract: Next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation aims to predict a user's next destination from spatio-temporal check-in data, and serves as the foundation for many location-based services. Recent advances incorporate large language models (LLMs) into this task by textualizing user trajectories to exploit their semantic reasoning ability. However, directly generating POI identifiers with such models is unreliable: POIs are sparse, localized, and long-tailed entities with weak natural-language semantics, which creates a semantic-to-entity gap between high-level mobility intent and concrete POI prediction. To bridge this gap, we propose ANCHOR, a category-anchored framework for semantic-to-entity grounding in next POI recommendation. Specifically, ANCHOR first estimates category-level mobility intent in a compact and stable semantic space, rather than predicting concrete POI entities directly. The inferred intent is then grounded into a candidate set by integrating three complementary sources of mobility evidence: category anchors, historical visit memory, and user preferences. Finally, a history-aware reranker selects the target POI by matching each candidate with the user's historical mobility patterns and current context. Experiments on three real-world check-in datasets show that ANCHOR consistently outperforms representative traditional, structure-enhanced, and LLM-based baselines on the reported metrics. Further analyses validate the effectiveness of semantic-to-entity grounding and show favorable trade-offs among candidate coverage, ranking quality, and inference efficiency.
